faqs.q: Do the rooms at Explora Rapa Nui have ocean views?
faqs.a: All rooms at Explora Rapa Nui have views to the gardens and the Pacific Ocean. The property sits on elevated grassland outside Hanga Roa, with the lodge oriented to take advantage of the island’s coastal landscape. Room views vary by specific location within the property — guests seeking a particular view orientation can request this at the time of booking.

faqs.q: Who designed Explora Rapa Nui?
faqs.a: Explora Rapa Nui was designed by Chilean architect José Cruz Ovalle. The architecture draws from the landscape and cultural heritage of Rapa Nui — the interconnected volumes of the building are described as echoing the arrangement of the island’s moai statues, while the use of natural wood and the interplay of shadow and light reflect the volcanic terrain. The design has received international architectural recognition.

faqs.q: Does Explora Rapa Nui have a pool?
faqs.a: Yes. Explora Rapa Nui has an outdoor swimming pool and hot tub, situated within the lodge grounds with views across the island’s grasslands toward the Pacific Ocean. The pool area is accessible to all guests as part of the all-inclusive stay. Pool hours and specific operating details can be confirmed with the property directly prior to arrival.

faqs.q: Does Explora Rapa Nui have a spa, and what treatments are available?
faqs.a: Yes. Explora Rapa Nui has a full-service spa — Hare Vaka — offering massage and body treatments, including options inspired by Polynesian and Rapa Nui wellness traditions. Basic spa facility access is included in the all-inclusive rate. Individual spa treatments are bookable separately and carry an additional charge. Appointments can be arranged prior to arrival or at the lodge.

faqs.q: Does Explora Rapa Nui have a sauna?
faqs.a: Yes. Explora Rapa Nui includes a sauna as part of the on-property wellness facilities. The sauna is available to all guests as part of the all-inclusive rate, alongside the outdoor pool, hot tub, and spa. Specific hours of operation can be confirmed with the property.

faqs.q: What are the views like at Explora Rapa Nui?
faqs.a: Explora Rapa Nui occupies elevated grassland on the outskirts of Hanga Roa, with sweeping views across the island’s volcanic landscape toward the Pacific Ocean. The lodge’s orientation and room placement are designed to maximize connection to the surrounding terrain. From the property, guests can see the coastline, open grasslands, and the wide Pacific horizon. The island’s archaeological sites and trailheads are accessible directly from the lodge.

faqs.q: What is the best hotel on Easter Island?
faqs.a: Explora Rapa Nui has been named among the best resorts in South America by the Condé Nast Traveler Readers’ Choice Awards and recognized as the World’s Leading Expedition Company. Located outside Hanga Roa with sweeping Pacific Ocean views, the lodge offers an all-inclusive experience focused on deep exploration of Rapa Nui culture, archaeology, and natural landscapes — a different category from conventional hotels on the island.

faqs.q: How do I get to Easter Island?
faqs.a: Easter Island (Rapa Nui) is served by Mataveri International Airport (IPC) in Hanga Roa. LATAM Airlines operates regular flights from Santiago, Chile (approximately 5 hours) and seasonal flights from Lima, Peru. Once you land, Explora coordinates round-trip airport transfers to and from the lodge as part of your all-inclusive rate. There are no connecting flights required — just one direct route from Santiago.

Options include hiking to the Rano Raraku moai quarry, biking to ancient ahu platforms, kayaking and stand-up paddleboarding along the volcanic coastline, snorkeling, diving, and cultural immersions with locally trained guides. Every exploration is customized daily based on your interests and fitness level.

faqs.a: Yes. The all-inclusive rate at Explora Rapa Nui covers all beverages, including Chilean wines, beer, and spirits, served throughout the day in the dining room and common areas. There is no separate bar tab or beverage charge during your stay. Premium or specialty selections beyond the standard offering may carry an additional cost — contact reservations for specifics prior to arrival.

faqs.q: What is not included in an Explora Rapa Nui stay?
faqs.a: The all-inclusive rate covers accommodations, all guided Explorations, all meals and beverages, spa facility access, national park entrance fees, and round-trip airport transfers. Items not included are personal purchases, gratuities, and optional spa treatments beyond general facility access. There are no hidden activity charges — every guided Exploration offered by Explora is included in the base rate.

faqs.a: Explora Rapa Nui has 30 rooms in total: 4 suites (including the Raa Suite at 44 m²/474 ft² with ocean and garden views) and 26 Varúa rooms (32 m²/345 ft²). All rooms include jetted bathtubs, twin or king bed configurations, and non-smoking policy. Room size reflects the lodge’s design philosophy: essential luxury and deep rest rather than maximalist features.

PATAGONIA NATIONAL PARK
Discover Myriad Wildlife
A visit to Patagonia National Park offers incredible wildlife viewing opportunities. A sanctuary born of critical rewilding and conservation efforts, the park is home to playful and photogenic guanacos as well as rare species like the endangered huemul deer and ñandú. Other notable wildlife includes condors, armadillos, foxes, and flamingos, all thriving in the park’s expansive grasslands and varied ecosystems. Though they pose no threat, you may be fortunate to also spot pumas silently patrolling the park.

sections.heading: Our Guides: Guardians of a Living Landscape
sections.text:
Our Guides: Guardians of a Living Landscape
Trained at our School of Guides, our bilingual experts carry a deep understanding of the territories we explore, grounded in geology, ecology, wildlife, and local culture.
They don’t just lead the way. They help you experience a rewilded Patagonia, a national park restored through the Tompkins conservation legacy, where overgrazed ranchland has returned to open steppe and native wildlife.
With a profound respect for the fragility of nature, our exceptional guides are also passionate advocates for conservation, adjusting every route with thoughtful attention to pace, weather, and terrain.

sections.heading: Four Areas of Exploration
sections.text:
Four Areas of Exploration
Ride an e‑bike, kayak on turquoise waters, cast a fly line into the Baker River or even soar by helicopter over the Northern Patagonian Ice Field. The options are endless with our unique explorations across four different zones of Patagonia National Park.

sections.heading: 1. Waters
sections.text:
Explore by: Hike Overland By air By water Combination E-Bike High Mountain Ascent
30 options to explore across 4 distinct zones:
1. Waters
The origin of all life lies in water. The action of glaciers, erosion, and more recently, streams and rivers like the Cochrane and Baker, have shaped a landscape that supports remarkable biodiversity. This environment is home to evergreen forests, birds like the Magellanic woodpecker, intricate fungal networks, and the elusive huemul, the southern Andean deer. Explore its glacier-fed rivers, with their turquoise hues, lakes, and wetlands that sustain this intricate web of life. Over time, human history has also intertwined with this vibrant ecosystem, sharing in and evolving alongside it.
Explore by: 
View Waters Explorations 
2. Veranadas
For the troperos - traditional nomadic herders - and ranchers of the region, the year was divided into two key seasons: the "veranada" and the "invernada. During the summer, the troperos drove their cattle to the veranadas, high pastures that, once free of snow, provided abundant grazing in clearings surrounded by deciduous forests of ñirre and lenga. In winter, the herds moved to the winter pastures, lower, sheltered areas where corrals provided protection from inclement weather. Today, thanks to the ecological restoration efforts led by Rewilding Chile, these clearings and ancient forests used for cattle grazing have been transformed into a natural sanctuary waiting to be explored.
Explore by: 
View Veranadas Explorations 
3. The Uplands
In the Aysén region, "el monte" describes the mountain areas beyond the forest line, where temperatures drop and vegetation disappears. This landscape of the Patagonian Andes, shaped by ancient glaciers, reveals Patagonia's vastness and untamed beauty from a unique perspective. For those wishing to explore the area's natural history and impressive geological formations, exploring this more challenging terrain is an ideal experience.

Explore its glacier-fed rivers, with their turquoise hues, lakes, and wetlands that sustain this intricate web of life. Over time, human history has also intertwined with this vibrant ecosystem, sharing in and evolving alongside it.

For the troperos - traditional nomadic herders - and ranchers of the region, the year was divided into two key seasons: the "veranada" and the "invernada. During the summer, the troperos drove their cattle to the veranadas, high pastures that, once free of snow, provided abundant grazing in clearings surrounded by deciduous forests of ñirre and lenga. Today, thanks to the ecological restoration efforts led by Rewilding Chile, these clearings and ancient forests used for cattle grazing have been transformed into a natural sanctuary waiting to be explored.

In the Aysén region, "el monte" describes the mountain areas beyond the forest line, where temperatures drop and vegetation disappears. This landscape of the Patagonian Andes, shaped by ancient glaciers, reveals Patagonia's vastness and untamed beauty from a unique perspective. For those wishing to explore the area's natural history and impressive geological formations, exploring this more challenging terrain is an ideal experience.

Framed by majestic mountains of many hues, the vast Chacabuco Valley stretches from east to west. Sculpted over millennia by geological forces and glacial activity, this breathtaking basin is now home to the Patagonian steppe, where guanacos roam free, pumas leave their tracks, and condors soar high above. The Chacabuco River Valley tells a story of enduring interaction between man and nature - once a refuge for ancient hunter-gatherer groups, and later a grazing ground for the vast herds of the estancia era. Today, its intricate network of trails invites explorers to discover a legacy of transformation, resilience and conservation.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.text:
Climate
Located in the heart of Chile’s Carretera Austral road, the climate of Chacabuco Valley, within Patagonia National Park, is defined by its striking seasonal contrasts and ever-present winds. Known for its dynamic weather changes, it’s not uncommon to experience sunshine, rain, and wind in a single day.
During the spring and summer months, from October to March, temperatures range from 50°F to 68°F (10°C to 20°C), with long daylight hours and plenty of time to explore. The fall months, beginning at the end of March, are a special time in the valley as the forests and grasslands burst into vibrant fall colors of red, yellow, and gold. This season, with cooler temperatures and crisp air, offers some of the most breathtaking scenery along the Carretera Austral road.
In winter, the famous Patagonian winds settle and the day becomes shorter, with temperatures ranging from -5°C to 5°C (23°F to 41°F). The varied climate throughout the year contributes to the region’s diverse ecosystems, creating an ever-changing backdrop for the park’s explorations.

sections.heading: FAQs
sections.text:
FAQs
HOW MANY NIGHTS DO YOU RECOMMED STAYING AT EXPLORA?
Considering the vast territory in which our lodge is situated, we recommend a minimum of five nights to have an exploration experience that allows you to deeply discover Patagonia National Park. However, we are confident that when you discover its wonders, you may want to extend your stay. Six nights is a great alternative to fully explore and enjoy the stunning landscapes.
CAN I CHANGE THE TYPE OF MY BED IN MY ROOM?
At the time of booking you must select a room with either a king size bed or two double beds. Being in the lodge, if you require, you may change your bed, subject to availability.
DO THE ROOMS COME WITH AIR CONDITIONING?
No, they only have heating.
AT WHAT TIME DO THE TRANSFER RUN BETWEEN AIRPORT AND EXPLORA?
Explora provides one transfer per day* from the airport to our lodge, a journey of approximately 5 hours along the stunning Carretera Austral, with much of the route being on unpaved roads. If your arrival time does not coincide with our transfers, we recommend staying one night in Coyhaique.
ARE TIPS INCLUDED?
No. At Explora tips are voluntary. If you wish to leave one, you can do so at reception at the end of your stay. It will be divided among all those who contributed to make your trip a unique experience. We suggest you leave USD$100 per day, per room.
WHAT ARE THE COORDINATES OF THE LODGE?

explorations.name: Valles Glaciares
explorations.text: An exploration that reveals the scale of the Northern Patagonian Ice Field from the air.

explorations.name: Baker
explorations.text: A full-day exploration of the Baker River begins at its outflow, where it empties its turquoise waters into the waters of Lake General Carrera. An overland journey leads us along the river, allowing us to discover the dynamic landscapes and transitions, crossing suspended bridges and tracing the river’s path to the sea, appreciating views of snow-capped peaks and ancient settlements.

explorations.name: Lago Gutierrez
explorations.text: This walking route recreates the ancient pathways of the Aonikenk, hunter-gatherers of Patagonia who roamed the pampas of the Chacabuco Valley thousands of years ago. Their traces endure in the petroglyphs of the Cueva de los Niños, located near the trail. The route culminates at Lago Gutiérrez, the largest in the Chacabuco Valley, which served as a resting site for the long journeys of nomadic Patagonian communities.

explorations.name: Tres Puentes
explorations.text: A dynamic e-bike ride along the winding slopes of the eastern Chacabuco Valley. Discover diverse landscapes ranging from expansive pampas and patches of ñirre and lenga forests to water bodies once used as rest stops for livestock transhumance, making this circuit filled with viewpoints a must-see for cycling and outdoor enthusiasts.

explorations.name: El Furioso
explorations.text: This trail offers stunning views of the Pampa Guanaco sector, with its iconic mountain formations that define the valley. Along the route, you'll encounter glaciolacustrine terraces that, thousands of years ago, provided refuge for hunter-gatherer societies that inhabited the eastern Patagonian region of Aysén.

explorations.name: Fly Fishing in the Baker River
explorations.text: We travel to Puerto Bertrand to embark on a cataraft along the Baker River. Surrounded by lush forests, turquoise waters, and snow-capped mountains, we begin our journey and fly-fishing adventure, aiming to catch the emblematic Patagonian trout using traditional fly-fishing techniques.

explorations.name: Northern Patagonian Ice Field
explorations.text: Discover the stunning landscapes of the Northern Patagonian Ice Field from above, flying in helicopter over the Laguna San Rafael National Park. This unique exploration lets you experience the majestic glaciers, mountains, valleys, rivers, and lakes of Northern Patagonia from a new perspective.

explorations.name: Borde Río
explorations.text: We leave by boat along the Cochrane river and lake basin, considered among the most crystalline waters in the world, until reaching the Correntadas sector, where we will hike along the southern slopes of the park through forests full of wildlife.

explorations.name: Aguas Claras
explorations.text: We leave by boat along the Cochrane River and lake basin, considered among the most crystalline waters in the world, observing the valley walls that make up part of the park. Different nothofagus species and livestock can be observed in the Tamango sector.

explorations.name: Gran Pasarela
explorations.text: We will bike across much of the Chacabuco Valley and the Patagonian steppe, observing how it has been recovering its original nature little by little. We will then continue up to the great walkway donated by Mr. Butler and get to know its interesting construction.

explorations.name: Laguna La Pepa
explorations.text: We will cycle along a trail with ascents and descents, from which we will see lagoons, ranches and nothofagus forests, until reaching Laguna La Pepa, which we will flank before returning along the same route.

explorations.name: Raices
explorations.text: We leave the lodge by van and head to the Laguna Edita sector, where we will begin our hike with a fairly steep hike up the steppe slopes of the Chacabuco Valley. After reaching the highest point, we will descend through a nothofagus forest where the silence is only interrupted by birdsong. In the end we reach Laguna Pepa, which surprises us with its deep blue color and views of the mountain ranges around it.

explorations.name: La Valchac
explorations.text: In this exploration we will focus on the Chacabuco River's valleys and route as a natural corridor traveled by nomadic peoples and diverse wildlife since ancestral times. We will discuss the anthropological and paleontological mysteries its rock formations hold, with caves and fossils that are vestiges of a past that it is still possible to bear witness to. These areas are characterized by their lack of snow in the summer and their low vegetation, devoid of trees. This allows you to observe a flat and open landscape where you can feel and live the icy southern wind. It is an experience among the vestiges of pre-Hispanic history and how they relate to the present and conservation.

explorations.name: La Vega
explorations.text: We leave the lodge on foot and take an introductory hike in Patagonia National Park on this exploration. We will begin in sectors where there are streams and low forests with significant presence of chacya (riparian shrub). As we enter the Park, we will begin to hear the songs of a variety of birds, such as churrin and bandurria tapaculo and black-faced ibis). Guanacos can be spotted grazing in this area.

explorations.name: Viaje Glaciar
explorations.text: We depart from Explora on the Patagonia National Park and travel along the Carretera Austral until taking back roads amid forests, rivers and lagoons until reaching the Calluqueo Glacier. This impressive tongue of ice hangs from the western slope of the solemn Mount San Lorenzo. It then flows into a murky glacial lagoon surrounded by walls of ice thousands of years old that impose themselves on the geography of the place. It is a natural environment that was formed over the course of centuries and millennia, where the scale of time is blurred. The wind causes the clouds surrounding Mount San Lorenzo to put on a shifting and dynamic show. We will be able to sit down and contemplate, walk around, or go down to get our wet feet in the lagoon.

explorations.name: Cañadón Chacabuco
explorations.text: We will leave the lodge on foot on a hike through large expanses of steppe, connecting with nature and wildlife. We will share amid the sound of birds and perhaps we will be able to glimpse the interaction between a puma and guanacos, part of this Patagonian territory.

explorations.name: Aves del Valle
explorations.text: The Patagonia National Park is a paradise for bird watching. On this exploration we cross a part of the Chacabuco Valley with great potential for observing diverse types of lagoon and river birds.

explorations.name: Confluencia
explorations.text: The confluence of the turquoise waters of the Baker River with the waters of the Chacabuco River is one of the iconic points of the Carretera Austral. We travel by van from the the lodge to witness the magnificent meeting of these two rivers and appreciate from a viewpoint how their colorful flows merge.

explorations.name: Sierra Guadal
explorations.text: We ascend through a region with varied ecosystems, where valleys, forests and plateaus contrast. The desert of the heights presents us with a scenery characteristic of the Patagonian mountains. The intense wind and the changing climate gave this exploration its name.

explorations.name: La Tejuela
explorations.text: We will visit a rancher's post to learn about part of the Chacabuco Valley's history. We will view its remains and get to now more about the lifestyle of its residents. We take a sloping path among ancient lenga forests, passing lagoons and diverse views. We will pass through transit areas used by huemuls and other species in the Patagonia National Park.

explorations.name: Oportus
explorations.text: We will cross a thick forest of ñirres and lengas. We will hike along a ridge with a view of the Chacabuco Valley and the Lake Cochrane basin. The marked summit offers a broad view as far as the northern ice field. It is named after Carlos Oportus, who in 1928 studied the situation and the possibilities for residents of the area. This hill reveals a spectacular part of the amazing Patagonia National Park from the heights.

explorations.name: La Leona
explorations.text: We cross the natural corridors of the Valleys with its contrasts their contrasts and sensations. Birds make their presence felt, as do the condors gliding in the heights. We will cross different environments until we come to an area with broad views of the valleys, some of them historic natural corridors in the area.

explorations.name: El Encuentro
explorations.text: We will leave the lodge on foot. We will hike up a trail that shows us the encounter between the Steppe and the Forest. As we go up we can appreciate the captivating Chacabuco Valley's slopes, amid hills and high-plateau lagoons. From Cerro Tamanguito we will have broad views of the Chacabuco Valley basin and Lake Cochrane.

explorations.name: Laguna Cisnes
explorations.text: We will hike through the steppe before arriving at a lagoon with one of the greatest variety of birds. There we can get to know the Patagonian fauna and observe the multitude of species that inhabit the area.

explorations.name: Las Correntadas
explorations.text: We will go to the Cochrane River rapids in kayak. We will walk to the Lake Cochrane viewpoint and return via the Los Carpinteros trail in the Tamango area. We will cross coigüe forests in the first half of the the exploration and then flank the riverbank with landscapes of pampa and Patagonian steppe. The difficulty level of this alternative is easy.

explorations.name: Caminantes
explorations.text: We will hike through the river valley to Lake Cochrane, which has one of the most crystalline waters in the world. We will contemplate the southern slopes of the Patagonia National Park, one of the main huemul habitats. We will visit the Huemul Post, the base for protecting and monitoring the huemules that transit through these areas. We will move through a forest full of birdsong and marked wildlife.

explorations.name: Los Pumas
explorations.text: We will leave the lodge on foot and hike through a vast steppe region bordering the Chacabuco River. This is one of the areas most populated by pumas and guanacos. Here we will learn more about these species and how to protect them.

explorations.name: Lagunas Altas
explorations.text: We will leave the lodge on foot and walk upward to view the valley from another perspective. The height reveals the mountains and plateaus that are interspersed with lagoons and forests. This is a very good option for birdwatching in the region as condors, eagles and other species can be seen.

explorations.name: Lago Chico
explorations.text: We will hike around the edge of Lago Chico, where forests, lagoons and ravines intertwine. We will have great views of Lake Cochrane and Cerro Oportus. Along the way different birds, part of the Patagonian fauna, can be seen.

explorations.name: Avilés
explorations.text: We will cross the Chacabuco Valley's natural corridors and as we move up we will see the different perspectives of contrasting landscapes around us. We can drink pure water from natural streams and get our feet wet crossing one of them. The silence of the landscape stands out in autumn and winter, contrasting with the birdsong that can be heard as background music for the rest of the year

## OVERVIEW
Journey to Explora Parque Nacional Patagonia
Created by Douglas and Kristine Tompkins, Patagonia National Park is an authentic hidden gem that exudes an intimate, peaceful and remote atmosphere. Here, nature flourishes in its most vibrant and thriving form, captivating visitors with pristine landscapes and extraordinary wildlife.
Located in the heart of Chile’s Carretera Austral, in a barely explored sector with majestic mountains, Chile’s fastest-flowing rivers and lakes with unique colors and clarity, the variety and number of explorations is practically unlimited.

You’re invited to embark on over 30 guided Explorations, included as part of your stay in Patagonia. Led by our expertly trained bilingual guides, these experiences and exclusive adventures include hiking to hidden mountain lagoons, e-biking among guanacos, kayaking on crystal-clear rivers, and breathtaking helicopter rides over ice fields. Every Exploration is customized daily to match your interests and fitness levels, promising a personalized adventure in Patagonia National Park.

Dine on Authentic Patagonian Cuisine
At Explora Parque Nacional Patagonia, enjoy a beautiful gastronomy experience that celebrates the region’s culinary traditions. Fresh, locally sourced ingredients and dishes highlighting Patagonia’s gaucho legacy are on offer, complete with Chilean wines, all of which are included as part of your stay.
VIEW MORE
Witness a Conservation Masterpiece
Douglas and Kristine Tompkins, renowned conservationists and former business leaders, spearheaded an unprecedented conservation effort in Patagonia that led to the creation in 2018 of Patagonia National Park. With a shared commitment to protect and explore responsibly, Explora invites you to experience this unique conservation success story at our sustainably designed lodge and alongside our knowledgeable and passionate local guides.
PATAGONIA NATIONAL PARK
Discover Myriad Wildlife
A visit to Patagonia National Park offers incredible wildlife viewing opportunities. A sanctuary born of critical rewilding and conservation efforts, the park is home to playful and photogenic guanacos as well as rare species like the endangered huemul deer and ñandú. Other notable wildlife includes condors, armadillos, foxes, and flamingos, all thriving in the park’s expansive grasslands and varied ecosystems. Though they pose no threat, you may be fortunate to also spot pumas silently patrolling the park.

Explore Chile’s Marble Caves on the Carretera Austral
The Explora Parque Nacional Patagonia journey begins in the captivating landscape of Chile’s legendary Carretera Austral road. The journey to our lodge, whether via overland vehicle or by air, passes by the jagged peaks of Cerro Castillo, turquoise lakes such as General Carrera, and pristine wilderness. Extend your time here and deepen your experience enroute by booking one night by the famed Marble Caves—a perfect prelude to the adventures that await at the lodge.

sections.heading: FAQs
sections.text:
FAQs
IS EXPLORA TORRES DEL PAINE ALL-INCLUSIVE?
Yes. Every Explora stay in Torres del Paine is fully all-inclusive. Your rate covers all accommodations, unlimited guided Explorations, all meals and beverages including Chilean wines and spirits, spa facility access, national park entrance fees, and round-trip transfers between Puerto Natales and the lodge. There are no supplementary charges for activities or guided experiences during your stay
WHAT IS INCLUDED IN AN EXPLORA TORRES DEL PAINE STAY?
Your stay includes accommodations in a 50-room lodge on the shores of Pehoé Lake, access to more than 40 guided Explorations — from treks to the iconic Towers to kayaking, horseback riding, and glacier hikes — all meals prepared by Explora’s culinary team, all beverages including wine, spa and pool access, national park entrance fees, and transfers. The only extras are personal purchases and optional spa treatments beyond the included facility access.
HOW DO I GET TO EXPLORA TORRES DEL PAINE FROM PUERTO NATALES?
Explora Torres del Paine is located approximately 112 kilometers (70 miles) north of Puerto Natales along Ruta 9 and the Sarmiento road into Torres del Paine National Park. The drive takes approximately 1.5 to 2 hours through Patagonian steppe and grasslands. Round-trip transfers between Puerto Natales and the lodge are included in every all-inclusive stay. Guests typically fly into Punta Arenas International Airport (PUQ), then travel to Puerto Natales by shuttle or private transfer before continuing to the lodge.
WHAT KINDS OF GUIDED EXPLORATIONS ARE AVAILABLE AT EXPLORA TORRES DEL PAINE?
Explora Torres del Paine offers more than 40 guided Explorations, all included in your stay. Options include day treks to the Base of the Towers (Las Torres), hikes to Grey Glacier, kayaking on the park’s lakes, birdwatching for condors and flamingos, horseback riding with a rare breed of Patagonian horses on Explora’s own reserve, and gaucho cultural experiences. Grand views! Native fauna represented by guanaco, rhea, puma, some birds whose name I don't know. If you go on a day trip have sufficient food and drink with you as pitstops are few and far between, selection limited, and prices exorbitant (if not extortionist). Torres del Paine National Park is a wonder to behold. It definitely feels like the remote end of the Earth. We rented a car and drove through the park taking lots of time to stop at the lookouts, take short hikes and see the guanacos and waterfalls. Although the roads are mostly dirt, with an all wheel drive vehicle, the flexibility of driving is a wonderful way to go. Take a map previously printed or download one to your phone because cell phone access is not available. We took a few wrong turns, but every misstep was an adventure.

Explore the Best of Torres del Paine
Choose from more than 40 guided Explorations across all six of Torres del Paine’s unique zones. Discover the famed granite pillars and Cuernos, autumnal forests, multi-colored lakes, and wildlife habitats where you may spot the guanaco and soaring Andean condor.

sections.heading: 1. Encuentro
sections.text:
Explore by: Hike Overland Horseback Ride High Mountain Ascent
Explore 34 destinations located in the 6 unique Torres del Paine zones:
1. Encuentro
The intersection, the estuary, the frontier. Sometimes the collision of two worlds is a world in itself. Convergence zones are places where two or more zones meet, generating unique characteristics product of their interaction. Explora is located within this area, on the shores of Lake Pehoé, with privileged views of the Paine Massif. From here you can partake in self-guided explorations or go by horse to nearby lookouts, the ultimate introduction to Patagonia. Chromatically unique, in the explorations around Lakes Pehoé, Toro and Nordenskjöld, shades of blue, green and grey appear due to centuries of glacial erosion and accumulation. At the end of the day we recommend visiting the Ona Bath House to contemplate the chromatic variations of dusk falling into night.
Explore by: 
View Encuentro Explorations 
2. Estepa
Only the Patagonian steppe is able to endure the relentless blow of the southern winds. This endurance portrays the character and courage of the people, past and present, who have inhabited these unusual lands throughout history. The open stretches of the Patagonian steppe dramatically contrast against the Paine Massif and the surrounding mountains, hosting a substantial part of the park’s wildlife. Traces of the ancient Aonikenk people can still be found in 4000-year-old cave paintings, which provide further inklings regarding their survival. Explorations in this area allow close encounters with the park’s wildlife: guanacos, rhea, foxes and even – if you’re lucky– the elusive puma.

Convergence zones are places where two or more zones meet, generating unique characteristics product of their interaction. Explora is located within this area, on the shores of Lake Pehoé, with privileged views of the Paine Massif. From here you can partake in self-guided explorations or go by horse to nearby lookouts, the ultimate introduction to Patagonia. Chromatically unique, in the explorations around Lakes Pehoé, Toro and Nordenskjöld, shades of blue, green and grey appear due to centuries of glacial erosion and accumulation. At the end of the day we recommend visiting the Ona Bath House to contemplate the chromatic variations of dusk falling into night.

Only the Patagonian steppe is able to endure the relentless blow of the southern winds. This endurance portrays the character and courage of the people, past and present, who have inhabited these unusual lands throughout history. The open stretches of the Patagonian steppe dramatically contrast against the Paine Massif and the surrounding mountains, hosting a substantial part of the park’s wildlife. Traces of the ancient Aonikenk people can still be found in 4000-year-old cave paintings, which provide further inklings regarding their survival. Explorations in this area allow close encounters with the park’s wildlife: guanacos, rhea, foxes and even – if you’re lucky– the elusive puma.

The gaucho and Patagonia are one, sharing temperance, silence, mystery and fascination. Trying to tell the story of this territory without their voice, is having completely misunderstood its essence. The Estancia 2 de Enero is a Patagonian ranch, property of Explora, where some of our most demanding horseback rides are held. The ranch is where – between October and April and depending on weather conditions – we hold the Quincho: a traditional Patagonian gathering in which the gauchos prepare a roast lamb overlooking the Paine granite towers. Conversation and laughter flow naturally as a mate is passed around among the gauchos and our guides, an ideal setting for camaraderie, laughter and spontaneous storytelling.

Forests disavow man made borders. Instead, drawing their own horizons – crossing mountains, skipping lakes and covering entire territories with patient vertical contemplation. In a landscape dominated by monumental geography and infinite open spaces, forests act as refuges and safe havens for the park’s fragile biodiversity. Some sectors of the forests are tall and majestic, whereas others are low-lying shrub, which stoically resist the harsh Patagonian winds. This area’s explorations lead us, among others, to the Rio Pingo Valley and the Ferrier hill, crossing lenga, ñirre and coigüe forests – species found only in Patagonia. Walking through these lands feeling the sounds of birds above and the murmur trees in the Patagonian wind is an experience that revitalizes the body and ignites the senses.

Glaciers are monuments of time. Patient titans of nature whose fragile presence is in great measure responsible for the geographic spectacle of Patagonia. This area’s explorations cross ancient nothofagus forests and tranquil lake beaches from which runaway glacial icebergs can be spotted nearby. A catamaran ride over the Grey Lake will take you to the Grey Glacier, part of the Southern Ice Fields, the third largest continental ice mass on the planet. From the Explora dock we sail across Lake Pehoé reaching the French Valley, gateway to the Paine massif’s heart. As you walk through the valley, dense forests of ñirre and lenga surround you, interrupted only by the watchful presence of the towering Paine Horns and the French glacier.

Mountains define local identity: a natural wall which only condors disregard, a presence which points to the stars above as the only vanishing point in the Patagonian landscape. Mountain explorations allow travelers to reach higher altitudes, crossing different ecosystems with distinctive wildlife and nature. Despite being more physically demanding, as a reward they offer spectacular views of the Paine Massif, the Southern Ice Fields, the Torres del Paine and the Chacabuco Mountain Range, among others. Well-equipped and willing to embrace the famous Patagonian wind, it’s possible to ascend to the granite amphitheater in the British camp, the base of the Torres del Paine or the summit of the Tenerife and Castillo hills.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.text:
Climate
Located in the so called Wet Andes –a climatic and glaciological sub region of the Andes mountain range– this part of Patagonia is mostly lush green, with a volatile climate that can spin all four seasons into a single day. This volatility translates in flora as varied as the climate itself, including dense forests, Patagonian steppe, mountainous scrubland and Andean desert. Likewise, the glaciers of the Wet Andes are far more stable than those of the Dry Andes due to summer precipitations, low thermal oscillations and overall high moisture.

sections.heading: FAQs
sections.text:
FAQs
WHAT EMERGENCY MEDICAL SERVICES ARE AVAILABLE?
All of our guides are Wilderness First Response (WFR) certified, guaranteeing that they have the necessary knowledge and abilities to aid people in remote locations.
In the Park administration, 15 minutes from the hotel, there is a paramedic stationed year round.
For more serious situations there is a hospital in Puerto Natales, 1.5 hours from the hotel, as well as the Clínica Magallanes in Punta Arenas, which is 5 hours from the hotel.
HOW CAN MY RELATIVES CONTACT ME IN CASE OF EMERGENCY?
Telephones (56 2) 3952580, (56 2) 3952581, (56 2) 3952582, fax (56 2) 3952584, or by email recpatagonia@explora.com.
HOW MANY NIGHTS DO YOU RECOMMEND STAYING AT EXPLORA?
We recommend a minimum of five nights to have an exploration experience that allows you to deeply discover Patagonia, although we are sure that when discovering the wonders of Torres del Paine National Park, you will feel like you needed more time. Six nights are a good alternative to achieve a more comprehensive knowledge of the area.
CAN I CHANGE THE TYPE OF MY BED IN MY ROOM?
At the time of booking you must select a room with either a king size bed or two double beds. Being in the lodge, if you require, you may change your bed, subject to availability.

explorations.text: The Cañadón de las Torres exploration takes its name from the landscape that defines it: a wide, open canyon that draws the gaze toward the imposing Torres, ever-present protagonists that set the course of the journey.

explorations.name: Puma Encounters
explorations.text: An exploration that invites you to responsibly observe pumas in their natural habitat. Accompanied by expert guides, you will explore the stunning landscapes of Patagonia and have the chance to observe this iconic feline. We invite you to experience the thrill of venturing into puma territory.

explorations.name: Horizonte
explorations.text: Discover one of the most scenic hikes in the Explora Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve. Explore lenga forests, sweeping views of the Paine Massif, and condor cliffs from the Obelisco Lookout.

explorations.name: Exploradores
explorations.text: We hike across the steppe of the reserve, surrounded by mountains, steppe and valleys. Aloong the way, you will be able to enjoy views of the Paine range, Cerro Obelisco, Laguna Jara and Sierra Baguales. The local flora is rich in coirón, matabarrosa and ñirre, while the fauna includes guanacos, pumas, chingues, caranchyos, condors and flamingoes, among others. In this area you can see the history of the occupation of the province of Última Esperanza, due to the old estate that was here. You will also learn about the history of Lady Florence Dixie, the first woman explorer in Patagonia.

explorations.name: El Pasado
explorations.text: We walked through the western sector of the Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve, with views of the Zamora Canyon and river, passing through Magellanic forests and rock monoliths. Throughout the journey, one can admire views of the impressive "V"-shaped canyon of the Zamora River and the Paine mountain range, including the Obelisco Hill. The local flora is rich in coiron, matabarrosa, lenga, mataguanacos, and nirre, while the fauna includes guanacos, pumas, chingues, caranchos, condors, bandurria, chuncho, among others.

faqs.q: Is Explora Torres del Paine all-inclusive?
faqs.a: Yes. Every Explora stay in Torres del Paine is fully all-inclusive. Your rate covers all accommodations, unlimited guided Explorations, all meals and beverages including Chilean wines and spirits, spa facility access, national park entrance fees, and round-trip transfers between Puerto Natales and the lodge. There are no supplementary charges for activities or guided experiences during your stay

faqs.q: What is included in an Explora Torres del Paine stay?
faqs.a: Your stay includes accommodations in a 50-room lodge on the shores of Pehoé Lake, access to more than 40 guided Explorations — from treks to the iconic Towers to kayaking, horseback riding, and glacier hikes — all meals prepared by Explora’s culinary team, all beverages including wine, spa and pool access, national park entrance fees, and transfers. The only extras are personal purchases and optional spa treatments beyond the included facility access.

faqs.q: How do I get to Explora Torres del Paine from Puerto Natales?
faqs.a: Explora Torres del Paine is located approximately 112 kilometers (70 miles) north of Puerto Natales along Ruta 9 and the Sarmiento road into Torres del Paine National Park. The drive takes approximately 1.5 to 2 hours through Patagonian steppe and grasslands. Round-trip transfers between Puerto Natales and the lodge are included in every all-inclusive stay. Guests typically fly into Punta Arenas International Airport (PUQ), then travel to Puerto Natales by shuttle or private transfer before continuing to the lodge.

faqs.q: What kinds of guided Explorations are available at Explora Torres del Paine?
faqs.a: Explora Torres del Paine offers more than 40 guided Explorations, all included in your stay. Options include day treks to the Base of the Towers (Las Torres), hikes to Grey Glacier, kayaking on the park’s lakes, birdwatching for condors and flamingos, horseback riding with a rare breed of Patagonian horses on Explora’s own reserve, and gaucho cultural experiences. Every Exploration is led by guides trained at Explora’s own School of Guides and customized to your fitness level and interests.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Torres del Paine?
faqs.a: The main trekking and expedition season in Torres del Paine runs from October through April (Southern Hemisphere spring through early fall). November to February offers the longest daylight hours and most stable weather, though wind is a constant factor year-round in Patagonia. Explora operates the lodge year-round; shoulder seasons (October–November and March–April) offer fewer visitors and lower rates while still providing full access to guided Explorations.

faqs.q: Is it better to stay inside Torres del Paine National Park or in Puerto Natales?
faqs.a: For travelers who want to maximize time in the park, staying inside is the better option. Puerto Natales is approximately 112 kilometers from the park entrance — a 1.5 to 2-hour drive each way — meaning a full day of exploration is lost for every night based in the city. Explora Torres del Paine is located inside the park on the shores of Pehoé Lake, with guided Explorations departing directly from the lodge each morning. Puerto Natales makes sense as a base for travelers on a tight budget or those doing a single day visit; for an all-inclusive expedition stay focused on depth of experience, the park lodge is the right choice.

faqs.q: Is Explora Torres del Paine suitable for non-hikers?
faqs.a: Yes. While the park is most famous for multi-day trekking routes like the W Trek, Explora’s program of 40+ guided Explorations goes well beyond hiking. Options for guests who prefer lower-intensity or non-hiking experiences include horseback riding on Explora’s private Conservation Reserve, kayaking on the park’s lakes, wildlife watching for pumas, condors, and guanacos, boat excursions to Grey Glacier, and gaucho cultural experiences. Explorations are matched to each guest’s interests and fitness level daily — a non-hiker can have a full, varied stay without setting foot on a technical trail.

faqs.q: Does Explora Torres del Paine have a spa?
faqs.a: Yes. Explora Torres del Paine has a full-service spa and wellness area that includes a heated indoor pool, steam sauna, and open-air hot tubs with views across the national park. Spa facilities are included in the all-inclusive rate. Individual spa treatments are available to book separately and carry an additional charge. Appointments can be arranged at the lodge during your stay.

faqs.q: What emergency medical services are available?
faqs.a: All of our guides are Wilderness First Response (WFR) certified, guaranteeing that they have the necessary knowledge and abilities to aid people in remote locations. In the Park administration, 15 minutes from the hotel, there is a paramedic stationed year round. For more serious situations there is a hospital in Puerto Natales, 1.5 hours from the hotel, as well as the Clínica Magallanes in Punta Arenas, which is 5 hours from the hotel.

IS EXPLORA TORRES DEL PAINE ALL-INCLUSIVE?

HOW DO I GET TO EXPLORA TORRES DEL PAINE FROM PUERTO NATALES?

Guests typically fly into Punta Arenas International Airport (PUQ), then travel to Puerto Natales by shuttle or private transfer before continuing to the lodge.

sections.heading: FAQs
sections.text:
FAQs
WHAT IS THE EXPLORA TORRES DEL PAINE CONSERVATION RESERVE AND HOW IS IT DIFFERENT FROM THE NATIONAL PARK?
The Explora Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve is a private 15,000-acre (6,000-hectare) protected wilderness located on the edge of Torres del Paine National Park in Chilean Patagonia — but not inside the park itself. This distinction makes the experience uniquely exclusive: guests explore landscapes virtually untouched by mass tourism, within a living territory actively managed for conservation and ecological restoration.
Part of the Torres del Paine Biosphere Reserve, this land is where native wildlife is actively returning, the steppe breathes freely, and gauchos maintain centuries-old Patagonian traditions. It offers a more private and personal refuge than a standard park lodge — a place to become part of the landscape rather than simply observe it.
WHAT GUIDED EXPLORATIONS ARE AVAILABLE AT EXPLORA TORRES DEL PAINE CONSERVATION RESERVE?
The lodge offers 30+ guided explorations across four distinct zones, from iconic national park landmarks to remote, rarely visited corners:
Macizo Paine — Trek to Base Torres, Valle Francés, and Glaciar Grey; access the park’s granite heart from unique angles via overland routes and navigation across Lago Pehoé.
Cuenca Paine — The quieter southeastern side of the park: open steppe, interconnected lakes (Laguna Azul, Lago Sarmiento), wetlands, and abundant wildlife including guanacos and Andean condors.
La Reserva — Explora’s private 6,000-hectare conservation territory: hike, ride horseback, or follow self-guided trails through lagoons, valleys, and former estancias.
Sierra Baguales — One of Patagonia’s most remote territories, with ancient fossil formations, vast valleys, and panoramic horizons near the Chile-Argentina border.
All explorations are led by bilingual certified guides trained at Explora’s own School of Guides, with groups limited to 8 guests for a deeply personal experience.

sections.heading: 1. Macizo Paine
sections.text:
Explore by: Hike Overland Horseback Ride Mountain Ascent
Explore 36 explorations located in the 4 unique Torres del Paine C. Reserve zones:
1. Macizo Paine
Reach the iconic granite massif from a completely different starting point. This zone covers the northwestern sector of Torres del Paine National Park, where the massif rises from the landscape to form some of Patagonia's most celebrated landmarks — the Torres del Paine, the Cuernos del Paine, and Glaciar Grey. Hike to the base of the Torres, trek through the legendary Valle Francés, and take in the towering walls of the Cuernos. Access combines overland routes and navigation across Lago Pehoé, revealing the massif from angles the classic circuits rarely show. These are the park's most iconic experiences — guided at Explora's pace: thoughtfully, unhurriedly, and with room for what the land itself wants to reveal.

sections.heading: Travel Tips
sections.text:
Travel Tips
Climate
Located in the so called Wet Andes –a climatic and glaciological sub region of the Andes mountain range– this part of Patagonia is mostly lush green, with a volatile climate that can spin all four seasons into a single day. This volatility translates in flora as varied as the climate itself, including dense forests, Patagonian steppe, mountainous scrubland and Andean desert. Likewise, the glaciers of the Wet Andes are far more stable than those of the Dry Andes due to summer precipitations, low thermal oscillations and overall high moisture.
Wifi & Voltage
Please note that due to our remote locations, Wi-Fi access in rooms and common areas may vary in reliability.
The voltage in Torres del Paine is 220V.
Tips
Tips are voluntary. If you wish to leave any, you can do so at the hotel reception at the end of your stay. It will be distributed among all those who contributed to making your trip a unique experience. We suggest leaving USD 100 per day per room.

explorations.name: Baguales
explorations.text: An overland journey into the Sierra Baguales through some of the most remote landscapes in Patagonia. Along the route, mountains and ravines reveal different layers of the area's history, until reaching Estancia Las Cumbres. From there, we walk through the surrounding terrain to grasp the scale and remoteness of this territory.

explorations.name: Vuelta a Baguales
explorations.text: Following the trails of Estancia Las Cumbres, the exploration ascends toward the upper reaches of this Patagonian mountain range. The route crosses the valleys of Cerro Redondo to circle around Cerro Torreón, passing near ancient high-mountain passes historically used as a link between Chile and Argentina. One of the most remote and immersive explorations in the territory.

explorations.name: Cerro Redondo
explorations.text: A mountain exploration in the Sierra Baguales that crosses landscapes dominated by ancient basaltic lavas, evidence of volcanic eruptions that transformed this region millions of years ago. As we gain elevation, the terrain becomes increasingly remote, with sweeping views across the Patagonian pampas and the mountains that mark the border with Argentina.

explorations.name: El Centinela
explorations.text: One of the most remote and least visited sectors of Torres del Paine National Park. The trail advances along the edge of a lagoon of deep blue hues, always accompanied by open views toward the Torres. As the valley deepens, the route gains elevation and the landscape grows wider and more solitary, revealing the scale and isolation of this part of the park.

explorations.name: Bandurria
explorations.text: This exploration traverses one of the most remote and striking landscapes of the Sierra Baguales. The trail follows the Bandurrias River valley, crossing hills shaped by ancient seas that covered this territory millions of years ago. Along the walk, a series of paddocks reveal the estancia history of the area.

explorations.name: Sierra Contreras
explorations.text: A mountain exploration that ascends toward one of the summits marking the boundary of the Reserve in the Sierra Contreras. The sierra formerly belonged to the estancias Santa Gemita and El Mercado, whose traces still form part of the ranching history of the area. The ascent crosses open slopes and ledges frequented by condors. From the summit, panoramic views of the reserve and the national park unfold.

explorations.name: Florence
explorations.text: A horseback exploration at trot and gallop. Alongside the guide and the gaucho, we ride through the three former estancias that gave rise to the current Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve. We cross rivers, open pampa, hills, and patches of forest. After fording the Las Chinas River, a steep ascent is followed by an equally demanding descent.

explorations.name: Tough Life
explorations.text: A horseback exploration at trot and gallop. Alongside the guide and the gaucho, we ride through the Conservation Reserve, crossing the grounds of the former estancias 2 de Enero and El Mercado. Along the way, we discover traces of the gaucho life that left its mark on these lands.

explorations.name: Cañadon las Torres
explorations.text: A wide open valley that draws the eye toward the Torres, setting the direction of the journey. Ancient grazing grounds are slowly giving way to the regeneration of native forest, a quiet process that reveals itself with every stretch of the trail. At an unhurried pace, we move through meadows, small lagoons, and natural viewpoints. The Torres appear and disappear among the hills.

explorations.name: Into the Wild
explorations.text: This exploration offers a closer look at the conservation and research work carried out within the Reserve. Through trails that cross steppe, wetlands, and meadows, we discover how camera traps are used to study wildlife — from small mammals and birds to guanacos and pumas. A way of reading and understanding the land through science.

explorations.name: Huellas de las Chinas
explorations.text: This exploration follows the course of the Las Chinas River, a natural corridor that has guided guanacos, hunters, and explorers for centuries. The trail crosses the Patagonian steppe, traces the riverbank, and reaches the waterfall that precedes its confluence with the Zamora River. From here, the Torres del Paine are also visible on the horizon, part of a landscape steeped in history.

explorations.name: Mirador del Obelisco
explorations.text: This walk ascends Cerro Obelisco through steppe, shrubland, and lenga beech forest, revealing views of the Paine massif and the Torres. To the north, the sheer walls of the Obelisco rise up, their rocky layers traced by soaring condors. After taking in the landscape, the descent brings you back on foot to the lodge.

explorations.name: Encuentros con el Puma
explorations.text: An exploration that invites you to observe, in a responsible manner, pumas in their natural habitat. Accompanied by expert guides, we explore the sweeping landscapes of Patagonia with the possibility of encountering this emblematic feline. Conducted in partnership with specialized external services, subject to availability.

explorations.name: Estepa Patagonica
explorations.text: In this exploration we board the van to traverse the most open areas of the park. Vast lakes such as Nordenskjöld and Sarmiento, dozens of lagoons that are home to diverse birds, waterfalls, and iconic mountains that shape the landscape. Throughout the journey, distant views of the Torres del Paine unfold and, with luck, sightings of local wildlife.

explorations.name: AONIKENK
explorations.text: The Aonikenk were the indigenous people who inhabited Patagonia before the arrival of the estancieros — hunter-gatherers who moved across the land following the guanacos, leaving traces of their passage throughout this territory. During the walk, it is also possible to discover fresh signs of pumas, condors, and guanacos.

explorations.name: Laguna Larga
explorations.text: This exploration offers one of the widest panoramic views of Torres del Paine. From here it is possible to identify the three great mountain groups — Paine Grande, the Cuernos, and Almirante Nieto — along with valleys such as the Francés and the Bader. The route combines open landscapes, Patagonian wildlife, lagoons, and geological features of interest.

explorations.name: Glaciar Grey
explorations.text: The exploration combines an overland journey and a navigation toward one of the most iconic glacial landscapes in Torres del Paine. From Playa Grey, a short walk through forest and lakeshore leads to the catamaran that ventures into the waters of Lake Grey, surrounded by icebergs calved from the glacier.

explorations.name: Valle del Silencio
explorations.text: This exploration ventures into a less-traveled valley of the Paine massif, following the route toward Campamento Japonés and the Valle del Silencio. The route offers views of the Torres from a perspective reserved almost exclusively for climbers, in a remote and silent setting. From here, other imposing mountains also come into view, such as Fortaleza, whose enormous walls often go unnoticed in the shadow of the Torres.

explorations.name: Desembocadura
explorations.text: This exploration crosses the open landscapes between Estancia Vega Castillo and the confluence of the Las Chinas River with Lake Toro. At this meeting point, extensive wetlands and small lagoons form, concentrating a rich diversity of birds and wildlife. The route traverses a particularly varied landscape, where steppe, wetlands, totora reeds, and forest interweave.

explorations.name: Vega Castillo
explorations.text: One of the most diverse wetlands in the southern sector of Torres del Paine, formed by remnant lagoons from the Last Glacial Maximum. These waters became trapped between ancient moraines, giving rise to a landscape where totora reeds, forest, steppe, and lagoons of varying depths interweave.

explorations.name: Fronteras
explorations.text: A horseback exploration, at a walking pace, through the Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve. Accompanied by a guide and a gaucho, we ride toward Laguna Jara, and from the highest point we can take in the vega wetland below — an area that shelters guanacos and a variety of Patagonian birds.

explorations.name: Laguna Rodas
explorations.text: This exploration traverses one of the most remote and striking landscapes of the Sierra Baguales. The trail follows the Bandurrias River valley, crossing hills shaped by ancient seas that covered this territory millions of years ago. Along the walk, a series of paddocks reveal the estancia history of the area.

explorations.name: Santa Gemita
explorations.text: This exploration leads into one of the former estancias that today form part of the Conservation Reserve. After crossing the Las Chinas River twice, the route advances through wide stretches of steppe to reach the old outpost of Santa Gemita, a shelter tied to Patagonian tradition. At these isolated outposts, it was customary to leave firewood, water, and food for the travelers who would come after. Along the walk, views also open toward Laguna Azul and the Torres del Paine.

explorations.name: Puente Malo
explorations.text: A ride at trot and gallop through the heart of the Reserve, circling a wetland known as La Vega. This area concentrates much of the reserve's wildlife thanks to the permanent presence of water. During the ride it is possible to spot local wildlife and cross the remains of an old bridge, which gives this exploration its name.

explorations.name: Base Torres
explorations.text: A mountainous terrain and forest with a continuous ascent alongside the Ascencio River to a glacial moraine of approximately 300 meters of elevation gain. Crossing that combination of landscapes, you reach the renowned viewpoint beside the lagoon, where a privileged view of the imposing Torres del Paine unfolds.

explorations.name: Fosiles
explorations.text: This exploration crosses one of the most fascinating paleontological areas of the Sierra Baguales. As we advance along the trail, we delve into the geological history of the territory, discovering how this landscape changed profoundly over time.

explorations.name: Valle Frances
explorations.text: A walk into the heart of the Paine mountains, tracing the valley that divides the imposing Cuernos and Paine Grande. Along the way, we take in close-up views of granite walls and glaciers, while crossing extensive areas of shrubland and forest.

explorations.name: Cuernos
explorations.text: This exploration traces the landscape between Lake Nordenskjöld and the imposing Cuernos del Paine, drawing close to the base of one of the most iconic mountains on the planet. At the foot of the massif, the trail reveals up close the immense scale of its granite walls and distinctive dark summits — a combination of sweeping views and direct proximity to the mountain.

explorations.name: La Loma
explorations.text: This exploration crosses an open stretch of steppe at the edge of the park, used in winter by guanacos as a breeding ground. The trail ascends slopes marked by ancient fires, revealing tracks and traces of the wildlife that has historically inhabited this area. From the ridge, a new perspective of the Paine massif opens up. The descent leads to Vega de los Ñandúes, a wetland rich in Patagonian birdlife.

explorations.name: Exploradores
explorations.text: A walk that allows you to explore the former grounds of an estancia that today forms part of the Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve. Its vast landscapes offer views of the Torres del Paine and the Sierra Baguales in the distance, along with traces of guanacos, condors, and pumas that have returned to inhabit this area.

explorations.name: Mirador Masle
explorations.text: Ascending through the slopes above the steppe, the exploration gains elevation to reveal one of the most iconic views of Torres del Paine: Laguna Azul in the foreground and, in the distance, the towers rising above the massif. From this vantage point, you take in the same perspective that captivated the first travelers who documented Patagonia in the late 19th century.

explorations.name: El Pasado
explorations.text: Following historic routes traced by gauchos and ranchers of the province, we will walk while observing the Zamora River from above. In the distance, the Torres del Paine stand out on the horizon from a wide and striking perspective.

explorations.name: Sarmiento
explorations.text: Thrombolites are white rocky formations found along the shores of Lake Sarmiento — evidence of some of the oldest organisms in the history of the planet, dating back more than 3.5 billion years. With the Paine mountains, the park's largest lake, and the Patagonian steppe as a backdrop, this exploration offers a glimpse into the origins of life on Earth.

explorations.name: Renacer
explorations.text: Setting out from the Lodge, the trail crosses a nothofagus forest to reach the heart of the reserve, where Laguna Jara awaits — an ecosystem that shelters both resident and migratory birds, including the Chilean flamingo.

explorations.name: El Humedal
explorations.text: The walk circles an expansive wetland formed by ancient lagoons and flooded areas that today shelter a rich diversity of Patagonian birds, drawn by the constant presence of water and vegetation. The combination of wetlands and sweeping views across the Paine landscape makes this exploration a quiet experience, ideal for wildlife observation and nature photography.

explorations.name: NORDENSKJÖLD
explorations.text: A trail with gentle ascents and descents leading to views of Lake Nordenskjöld, whose intensely colored glacial waters stretch out before the imposing Cuernos del Paine, the Francés valley, and Paine Grande.

faqs.q: What is the Explora Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve and how is it different from the National Park?
faqs.a: The Explora Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve is a private 15,000-acre (6,000-hectare) protected wilderness located on the edge of Torres del Paine National Park in Chilean Patagonia — but not inside the park itself. This distinction makes the experience uniquely exclusive: guests explore landscapes virtually untouched by mass tourism, within a living territory actively managed for conservation and ecological restoration. Part of the Torres del Paine Biosphere Reserve, this land is where native wildlife is actively returning, the steppe breathes freely, and gauchos maintain centuries-old Patagonian traditions. It offers a more private and personal refuge than a standard park lodge — a place to become part of the landscape rather than simply observe it.

faqs.q: What guided explorations are available at Explora Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve?
faqs.a: The lodge offers 30+ guided explorations across four distinct zones, from iconic national park landmarks to remote, rarely visited corners: Macizo Paine — Trek to Base Torres, Valle Francés, and Glaciar Grey; access the park’s granite heart from unique angles via overland routes and navigation across Lago Pehoé. Cuenca Paine — The quieter southeastern side of the park: open steppe, interconnected lakes (Laguna Azul, Lago Sarmiento), wetlands, and abundant wildlife including guanacos and Andean condors. La Reserva — Explora’s private 6,000-hectare conservation territory: hike, ride horseback, or follow self-guided trails through lagoons, valleys, and former estancias. Sierra Baguales — One of Patagonia’s most remote territories, with ancient fossil formations, vast valleys, and panoramic horizons near the Chile-Argentina border. All explorations are led by bilingual certified guides trained at Explora’s own School of Guides, with groups limited to 8 guests for a deeply personal experience.

faqs.q: What is included in a stay at Explora Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve?
faqs.a: A stay is fully all-inclusive, covering everything needed for an immersive Patagonian experience: 10 intimate rooms with views of the Torres del Paine peaks or native forest All guided explorations — 30+ daily excursions on foot, horseback, overland, and self-guided trails All meals and beverages — Patagonian-inspired cuisine including traditional asados prepared by reserve gauchos, paired with Chilean wines Spa facilities — outdoor hot tubs and massage room National Park entrance fees Round-trip transfers from Puerto Natales according to preset schedules The only additional costs are flights, optional private transfers, and personal expenses.

faqs.q: How do I get to Explora Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve?
faqs.a: The main gateway is Puerto Natales, Chile. From there, the lodge is approximately a 2-hour drive (mostly paved road, with only 20 km of gravel). How to reach Puerto Natales: From Santiago, Chile — Direct flights with LATAM or Sky Airlines to Puerto Natales Airport. Explora provides complimentary van transfers from the airport (pick-up at 12:00 or 15:00) or from Puerto Natales hotels (11:00–12:00). From El Calafate, Argentina — Overland transfer (approx. 5–6 hours, 374 km), crossing the Chile-Argentina border. Available on select days October–April. From Patagonia National Park (Chile) — An exclusive 1.5-hour lodge-to-lodge flight over the Andes and the Southern Ice Field, available Mondays and Thursdays from October to mid-April (for programs with transfer included). From El Chaltén, Argentina — Overland transfer (approx. 8–9 hours, 402 km), available for guests combining stays.

faqs.q: What is the climate like at Torres del Paine and when is the best time to visit?
faqs.a: Torres del Paine sits in the “Wet Andes” — a climatic sub-region known for its volatile, rapidly changing weather. It’s famously said that you can experience all four seasons in a single day. This volatility is what creates the region’s extraordinary diversity: dense forests, Patagonian steppe, mountainous scrubland, and the spectacular glaciers of the Southern Patagonian Icefield — most retreating in response to climate change, an evidence of the region’s ecological fragility. Summer (November–February): The most popular season — long days, wildflowers, and the best conditions for iconic treks like Base Torres and Valle Francés. Autumn (March–May): Arguably the most beautiful — golden and red foliage across the beech forests, calmer winds, fewer visitors. Winter (June–August): A serene, solitary experience with snow-dusted peaks and very few crowds. The reserve’s glaciers appear dramatic under pale winter light. Spring (September–October): Wildlife activity peaks, days lengthen rapidly, and the landscape transitions from winter grey to vibrant green. The lodge is open year-round, and each season reveals a completely different face of Patagonia.

faqs.q: What makes Explora's conservation work at Torres del Paine unique?
faqs.a: Explora’s commitment to conservation goes beyond responsible tourism — it is the core purpose of the Reserve itself. Spanning nearly 15,000 acres (6,000 hectares), the Reserve is part of the Torres del Paine Biosphere Reserve and is managed under an active philosophy of ecological restoration and regeneration. This means guests don’t just visit a protected landscape — they become part of a living conservation project where: Native wildlife is actively returning to previously degraded land Gaucho traditions are preserved as part of the cultural and ecological fabric of the territory Explora’s park rangers and guides are trained with deep local knowledge and a genuine commitment to protecting the fragility of this extraordinary place Responsible travel, science, and local culture work together to safeguard one of Earth’s most iconic wilderness areas Staying at the Conservation Reserve is a way to travel with purpose — where every exploration leaves the land better than you found it.

text:
## OVERVIEW
Welcome to Explora Torres del Paine - Conservation Reserve
Welcome to our new lodge, an exclusive Patagonian sanctuary nestled on the edge of Torres del Paine National Park. Here, profound silence stretches across the vast steppe, native wildlife roams freely, and the iconic peaks rise beyond endless horizons. This privileged location is your gateway to exploring both the park’s most celebrated landmarks and its pristine, almost unexplored corners.
The Best Hotels & Resorts in the World: The Gold List 2025
World's Leading Expedition Company 2025
Conservation Sustainability with Soul
Beyond Luxury: Immerse Yourself in the Patagonian Wild
Designed for intimacy and immersion, the lodge features just ten rooms overlooking the Patagonian steppe and the towering Torres peaks. Inside, warm, inviting interiors, serene spaces, and an outdoor hot tubs and massage room offer a peaceful sanctuary after a day of discovery and exploration. Here, luxury is measured not by opulence, but by silence, remoteness, and a genuine connection with Patagonia’s landscapes and rhythms.

Explore the Iconic and the Untamed
The journey begins from the heart of our Conservation Reserve, a gateway to Patagonia’s wildest landscapes. Explore the park’s classic landmarks, from the legendary Towers Base to the French Valley, yet venture beyond the well-trodden paths to discover the northern reaches of the park—places few have ever seen. Choose your way to explore: on foot, on horseback, overland, or on self-guided adventures, each offering a unique way to connect with this extraordinary land, where nature, culture and conservation meet.
VIEW EXPLORATIONS
CHECK AVAILABILITY
The Stables and Horses of the Reserve
The stables at the Explora Conservation Reserve are home to horses specially bred and trained for the wild Patagonian terrain. Under the care of our skilled gauchos—their devoted guardians—these horses capture the spirit of the land and the heritage of the region. Riding through the steppe is part of Patagonia’s soul, and we invite you to experience from the saddle,—discovering Patagonia just as the gauchos have for generations.
DINING
Intimate Dining with Patagonian Flavors

From seasonal menus to traditional asados at the quincho prepared by our reserve gauchos, every dining experience is rooted in the region’s land and culture. Ingredients are locally sourced whenever possible, offering travelers a true taste of this vast territory—simple, genuine, and deeply connected to its origins. And don’t forget to pair it all with some of Chile’s world-renowned wines.

The Explora Conservation Reserve lies at the core of our mission to protect and restore Patagonia’s unique ecosystems. Spanning nearly 15,000 acres (6,000 hectares), and part of the Torres del Paine Biosphere Reserve, it stands as a living example of how responsible travel, science, and local culture can come together to safeguard one of the planet’s most iconic wilderness areas.

With over 30 years of expertise and a unique network of five lodges and one expedition—each interconnected across Chile and Argentina—we invite travelers to experience the region as a single, continuous journey. From the southern fjords and windswept steppes to the soaring peaks of Torres del Paine and El Chaltén, every destination reveals a different face of Patagonia, united by a deep spirit of exploration.

It provides a more private and personal refuge than our other lodges, where travelers go beyond observing the landscape to become part of its rhythm and essence.
Secluded Within a Living Conservation Reserve
Just two hours from Puerto Natales, Chile, our lodge lies at the center of the Explora Conservation Reserve—nearly 15,000 acres (6,000 hectares) of protected Patagonian wilderness. Set within a working reserve managed by Explora, it is surrounded by active conservation projects, native wildlife, and the enduring traditions gaucho life.
Here, horses graze freely, the aroma of traditional Patagonian flavors fills the quincho, and the vast steppe streches endlessly toward the horizon – an ever-changing landscape of light, silence, and boundless discovery.

FAQs
WHAT IS THE EXPLORA TORRES DEL PAINE CONSERVATION RESERVE AND HOW IS IT DIFFERENT FROM THE NATIONAL PARK?
The Explora Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve is a private 15,000-acre (6,000-hectare) protected wilderness located on the edge of Torres del Paine National Park in Chilean Patagonia — but not inside the park itself. This distinction makes the experience uniquely exclusive: guests explore landscapes virtually untouched by mass tourism, within a living territory actively managed for conservation and ecological restoration.
Part of the Torres del Paine Biosphere Reserve, this land is where native wildlife is actively returning, the steppe breathes freely, and gauchos maintain centuries-old Patagonian traditions. It offers a more private and personal refuge than a standard park lodge — a place to become part of the landscape rather than simply observe it.
WHAT GUIDED EXPLORATIONS ARE AVAILABLE AT EXPLORA TORRES DEL PAINE CONSERVATION RESERVE?
The lodge offers 30+ guided explorations across four distinct zones, from iconic national park landmarks to remote, rarely visited corners:
Macizo Paine — Trek to Base Torres, Valle Francés, and Glaciar Grey; access the park’s granite heart from unique angles via overland routes and navigation across Lago Pehoé.
Cuenca Paine — The quieter southeastern side of the park: open steppe, interconnected lakes (Laguna Azul, Lago Sarmiento), wetlands, and abundant wildlife including guanacos and Andean condors.
La Reserva — Explora’s private 6,000-hectare conservation territory: hike, ride horseback, or follow self-guided trails through lagoons, valleys, and former estancias.
Sierra Baguales — One of Patagonia’s most remote territories, with ancient fossil formations, vast valleys, and panoramic horizons near the Chile-Argentina border.

FAQs
FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS
WHAT AIRPORT DO YOU FLY INTO FOR THE SACRED VALLEY AND MACHU PICCHU?
The primary gateway is Alejandro Velasco Astete International Airport in Cusco (CUZ), approximately 90 kilometers from Explora Valle Sagrado in the Sacred Valley. Cusco is served by direct flights from Lima (LIM), with a flight time of approximately 1 hour 20 minutes. Most luxury lodges in the Sacred Valley, including Explora Valle Sagrado, arrange round-trip airport transfers from Cusco; transfers should be confirmed at the time of booking. The drive from Cusco Airport to the lodge takes approximately 1.5 to 2 hours through the Andean highlands. Machu Picchu itself has no commercial airport; the standard access route is by train from Cusco or Ollantaytambo to Aguas Calientes.
WHAT IS THE BEST TIME OF YEAR TO VISIT THE SACRED VALLEY AND MACHU PICCHU?
The Sacred Valley and Machu Picchu are year-round destinations, with each season offering different conditions. May through October is the dry season, with clear skies, cooler temperatures, and the most stable weather for trekking and high-altitude explorations — this is peak season for both destinations. June through August sees the highest visitor demand; advance booking is strongly recommended. November through April is the wet season, with more rainfall but lush green landscapes, fewer crowds, and generally lower rates at luxury lodges. Brief afternoon showers are common during this period but rarely disrupt full-day programs. Advance booking is recommended regardless of season, as capacity at luxury lodges is limited year-round.
WHAT IS INCLUDED IN A SACRED VALLEY ALL-INCLUSIVE PACKAGE?
At Explora Valle Sagrado, the all-inclusive rate covers accommodation, all meals prepared with local Andean ingredients, non-alcoholic beverages, and more than 40 guided explorations each day. sections.heading: FAQs
sections.text:
FAQs
FAQS
IS EXPLORA VALLE SAGRADO ADULTS-ONLY?
No. Explora Valle Sagrado welcomes guests of all ages, including families with children. Explorations are customized daily by interest and fitness level, making them accessible across different age groups and abilities. The outdoor swimming pool and hot tubs are popular with younger guests. Cribs and extra beds for children are available on request. Families traveling with young children are encouraged to discuss exploration planning with Explora at booking to ensure a schedule that works well for everyone.
DOES EXPLORA VALLE SAGRADO INCLUDE ALCOHOL?
Alcoholic beverages are not included in the standard all-inclusive rate. The rate covers accommodation, all meals, non-alcoholic beverages, more than 40 guided explorations, and access to the spa facilities, pool, and hot tubs. Wine, beer, and spirits are available at the bar and restaurant and charged separately. Individual spa treatments are also available at an additional cost and are recommended to be booked in advance directly with the lodge.
DO YOU GET ALTITUDE SICKNESS AT EXPLORA VALLE SAGRADO?
Explora Valle Sagrado sits at 9,514 feet (2,900 meters) above sea level, above the general threshold where some visitors begin to notice mild altitude effects such as headaches, fatigue, or shortness of breath. Most guests acclimatize comfortably within one to two days. Some explorations reach higher elevations, including Cusco at approximately 11,200 feet (3,400 meters). Staying well-hydrated, avoiding alcohol on arrival, and resting on the first afternoon are generally recommended. Guests with a history of altitude sensitivity are encouraged to consult a physician before travel.
