sections.heading: 1. Janca
sections.text:
Explore by:
Our Exploration Zones
1. Janca
Towering titans that reach into the clouds above, defying altitude and gravity in order to provide a vital experience of heaven on Earth for all who venture their slopes. Janca is the highest part of the Peruvian Andes. Its inaccessibility simultaneously defines its essence and beauty. Due to the zone’s extreme altitude, life acquires a calmer pace; human settlements are scarce and dedicated mainly to high mountain mining. Reaching the Janca zone requires special acclimatization due to the area’s extremely low temperatures and lack of oxygen. Likewise, this zone is mostly steep terrain, which requires technical knowledge and experience.
Explore by: 
View Janca Explorations 
2. Quechua
The Quechua zone is the starting point for all our explorations in the Sacred Valley. Following the winding course of the Urubamba River, this area showcases Inca architecture at its best, enclosing some of Peru’s most important archaeological landmarks, from Pisac to Macchu Picchu. As we ascend progressively through cornfields, orchards and small villages bustling with life, we reach some of the most enigmatic and remote archaeological sites of the valley, as is Pumamarca, a hillside fortress that once guarded the entrance to the valley’s fertile lands.
Explore by: 
View Quechua Explorations 
3. Suni
With the valley at its feet, Suni is a transition zone between the Quechua and Puna zones. Within, some of the area’s most memorable panoramic views can be found from winding paths perched high on deep gorges plunging into the green abyss below. This zone showcases the valley’s verticality – a pivotal component around which the Incas developed their particular cosmovision. Technological development and communal work structures can be evidenced in the extremely well-preserved ruins of the Moray experimental crop center and the Salineras de Maras, as well as the precision and craftsmanship of Tipon’s fluvial canals, which remain active to this day.

Technological development and communal work structures can be evidenced in the extremely well-preserved ruins of the Moray experimental crop center and the Salineras de Maras, as well as the precision and craftsmanship of Tipon’s fluvial canals, which remain active to this day.

Abruptly rising from the ground beneath your feet, mountains define almost every aspect of the Sacred Valley’s identity. As they grow in height the sheer power of altitude, combined with the cold from the perpetual glaciers perched high on their rugged shoulders, are proof of how living conditions become harsher the further from the ground you dare to go. Explorations in the area of the Puna take travelers through narrow shepherd mountain trails and chromatic progressions of green, brown and white. This highly dynamic zone is a feast to the eyes that varies significantly depending on the seasons and harvesting times.

For centuries, Cusco and the Sacred Valley of the Incas have been a crossroads of paths, cultures and travelers, and for many explorers, they remain their first encounter with Peru.

sections.heading: Climate
sections.text:
Climate
Cusco’s high altitude and proximity to the Equator create a diverse climate with two main seasons, each offering its own unique experiences.
From April to October, the dry season features plenty of sunshine and occasional night frosts. July is the coldest month, with average temperatures around 49.5°F (9.7°C). The rainy season, from November to March, brings warmer average temperatures of 55.9°F (13.3°C) and sporadic, moderate showers typical of the region’s subtropical climate. Throughout the year, temperatures range from 32.4°F (0.2°C) to 69.6°F (20.9°C), with occasional extremes reaching as low as 16°F (-8.9°C) or as high as 86°F (30°C).

sections.heading: FAQs
sections.text:
FAQs
FAQS
HOW IS THE CLIMATE IN CUSCO AND WHEN IS THE BEST TIME TO TRAVEL?
The Sacred Valley enjoys two distinct seasons, each with its own character and appeal — shaped by the region’s high altitude and proximity to the equator.
Dry Season (April – October)
This is the sunniest time of year, with clear skies and crisp mountain air. The landscape takes on warm shades of yellow and ochre as the Andean plains dry out. Temperatures are pleasant during the day, ranging from 41°F to 68°F (5°C to 20°C), though nights can be cold and occasional frosts are not uncommon, sometimes dropping to 32°F (0°C).
Wet Season (November – March)
The valley transforms into a lush, vivid green as rainfall brings the landscape to life. The atmosphere is warmer and more subtropical, with temperatures ranging from 45°F to 70°F (7°C to 21°C). While rain is frequent, it rarely lasts all day — mornings are often clear, and the light during this season is particularly beautiful.
Both seasons offer genuinely rewarding experiences, and the “best” time to visit ultimately depends on the kind of landscape and atmosphere you’re drawn to. We’re happy to help you decide based on your preferences.
HOW MANY NIGHTS DO YOU RECOMMEND STAYING AT EXPLORA SACRED VALLEY?
We recommend a minimum of five nights to truly experience the Sacred Valley. The region is remarkably diverse, and a shorter stay simply doesn’t allow enough time to explore its many hidden corners and lesser-known sites.
For those wishing to include our full-day explorations to Machu Picchu or Cusco — two of the highlights of any visit to this region — five nights is the baseline we suggest. If you’d like a deeper, more unhurried experience of both the Sacred Valley and the greater Cusco region, six nights is an excellent choice.

faqs.q: What airport do you fly into for the Sacred Valley and Machu Picchu?
faqs.a: The primary gateway is Alejandro Velasco Astete International Airport in Cusco (CUZ), approximately 90 kilometers from Explora Valle Sagrado in the Sacred Valley. Cusco is served by direct flights from Lima (LIM), with a flight time of approximately 1 hour 20 minutes. Most luxury lodges in the Sacred Valley, including Explora Valle Sagrado, arrange round-trip airport transfers from Cusco; transfers should be confirmed at the time of booking. The drive from Cusco Airport to the lodge takes approximately 1.5 to 2 hours through the Andean highlands. Machu Picchu itself has no commercial airport; the standard access route is by train from Cusco or Ollantaytambo to Aguas Calientes.

faqs.q: What is the best time of year to visit the Sacred Valley and Machu Picchu?
faqs.a: The Sacred Valley and Machu Picchu are year-round destinations, with each season offering different conditions. May through October is the dry season, with clear skies, cooler temperatures, and the most stable weather for trekking and high-altitude explorations — this is peak season for both destinations. June through August sees the highest visitor demand; advance booking is strongly recommended. November through April is the wet season, with more rainfall but lush green landscapes, fewer crowds, and generally lower rates at luxury lodges. Brief afternoon showers are common during this period but rarely disrupt full-day programs. Advance booking is recommended regardless of season, as capacity at luxury lodges is limited year-round.

faqs.q: What is included in a Sacred Valley all-inclusive package?
faqs.a: At Explora Valle Sagrado, the all-inclusive rate covers accommodation, all meals prepared with local Andean ingredients, non-alcoholic beverages, and more than 40 guided explorations each day. Access to the Pumacahua Spa and Bath House, saunas, steam baths, an outdoor swimming pool, and hot tubs is also included. Round-trip airport transfers from Cusco are arranged by Explora. A full-day visit to Machu Picchu can be arranged as an extension to any stay; applicable entry permit and train transport fees may apply separately.

faqs.q: Do Sacred Valley lodges include airport transfers from Cusco?
faqs.a: Most luxury all-inclusive lodges in Peru’s Sacred Valley, including Explora Valle Sagrado, arrange airport transfers from Cusco (CUZ). At Explora, transfers are organized by the lodge and should be confirmed at the time of booking. The drive from Cusco Airport to Explora Valle Sagrado takes approximately 1.5 to 2 hours through the Andean highlands. Transfer inclusions and any associated costs vary by property; verify directly with your lodge at the time of reservation.

faqs.q: How many nights should I plan for the Sacred Valley?
faqs.a: Most travel specialists recommend a minimum of four to five nights in the Sacred Valley to experience a meaningful range of Inca sites and exploration zones. Explora recommends five nights as a minimum; additional nights allow time to acclimatize to the altitude, complete a full-day visit to Machu Picchu, and explore lesser known sites such as Chinchero, Moray, and the Maras salt mines. Travelers planning a Machu Picchu visit typically combine three to four nights in the Sacred Valley with a dedicated day trip or overnight in Aguas Calientes.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of the Sacred Valley?
faqs.a: Explora Valle Sagrado is situated at approximately 9,514 feet (2,900 meters) above sea level near the village of Urubamba. Cusco, the main gateway city, sits at approximately 11,200 feet (3,400 meters). Machu Picchu is considerably lower, at approximately 7,970 feet (2,430 meters). Altitude effects such as headache, fatigue, or shortness of breath are common for newly arrived visitors. Most guests acclimatize within one to two days; staying well-hydrated, avoiding strenuous activity on arrival, and limiting alcohol on the first evening are generally recommended.

faqs.q: Can I visit Machu Picchu from Explora Valle Sagrado?
faqs.a: Yes. Explora Valle Sagrado is an ideal base for a full-day visit to Machu Picchu. The standard route involves a train from Ollantaytambo to Aguas Calientes (approximately 1.5 to 2 hours) followed by a short bus ride to the Machu Picchu entrance (approximately 30 minutes). Entry to Machu Picchu is controlled through a government permit system with daily visitor caps, timed entry windows, and phased ticket releases. During peak season — May through August — available slots regularly sell out within hours of release, and the most popular entry times (early morning) go first. Booking six to eight weeks ahead is standard for peak-season visits; last-minute access is not reliable. Explora’s planning team coordinates your entry permit, train from Ollantaytambo to Aguas Calientes, and guided site access as part of your stay — the logistics are handled in advance so guests arrive with confirmed access rather than contingency plans.

faqs.q: Is it better to stay in the Sacred Valley or in Cusco for a Machu Picchu visit?
faqs.a: The Sacred Valley offers a meaningful logistical advantage over Cusco for travelers prioritizing Machu Picchu access. The Ollantaytambo train station — the primary departure point for Aguas Calientes — is within the Sacred Valley, reducing morning travel time on the day of your Machu Picchu visit compared to departing from Cusco. Sacred Valley lodges also sit at a lower elevation than Cusco (approximately 9,500 feet vs. 11,200 feet), which benefits guests who are sensitive to altitude. Cusco provides more urban amenities and a wider range of restaurants and independent excursions. Travelers combining Machu Picchu access with sustained Andean exploration — including multiple Inca sites across the Sacred Valley — typically find an all-inclusive lodge in the Sacred Valley the more efficient and immersive base.

faqs.q: Do Sacred Valley lodges include guided explorations in the rate?
faqs.a: Inclusion policies vary by property. At Explora Valle Sagrado, more than 40 guided explorations are included in the all-inclusive rate, led by Explora’s own bilingual guides trained at the company’s in-house School of Guides. Explorations are customized each day to your interests and fitness level and cover sites across the Inca heartland, including Pisac, Ollantaytambo, Moray, the Maras salt mines, and a full-day visit to Machu Picchu. Many Sacred Valley boutique hotels do not include guided excursions in their nightly rate — activities are typically booked separately through local operators. If guided access to archaeological sites is a priority, verify inclusions directly with your property at the time of booking.

faqs.q: Is Explora Valle Sagrado adults-only?
faqs.a: No. Explora Valle Sagrado welcomes guests of all ages, including families with children. Explorations are customized daily by interest and fitness level, making them accessible across different age groups and abilities. The outdoor swimming pool and hot tubs are popular with younger guests. Cribs and extra beds for children are available on request. Families traveling with young children are encouraged to discuss exploration planning with Explora at booking to ensure a schedule that works well for everyone.

faqs.q: Does Explora Valle Sagrado include alcohol?
faqs.a: Alcoholic beverages are not included in the standard all-inclusive rate. The rate covers accommodation, all meals, non-alcoholic beverages, more than 40 guided explorations, and access to the spa facilities, pool, and hot tubs. Wine, beer, and spirits are available at the bar and restaurant and charged separately. Individual spa treatments are also available at an additional cost and are recommended to be booked in advance directly with the lodge.

faqs.q: Do you get altitude sickness at Explora Valle Sagrado?
faqs.a: Explora Valle Sagrado sits at 9,514 feet (2,900 meters) above sea level, above the general threshold where some visitors begin to notice mild altitude effects such as headaches, fatigue, or shortness of breath. Most guests acclimatize comfortably within one to two days. Some explorations reach higher elevations, including Cusco at approximately 11,200 feet (3,400 meters). Staying well-hydrated, avoiding alcohol on arrival, and resting on the first afternoon are generally recommended. Guests with a history of altitude sensitivity are encouraged to consult a physician before travel.

faqs.q: What is included in a stay at Explora Valle Sagrado?
faqs.a: A stay includes accommodation, all meals and non-alcoholic beverages, and more than 40 guided explorations each day. Access to the Pumacahua Spa and Bath House, saunas, steam baths, outdoor swimming pool, and hot tubs is included. Explorations are customized daily to your interests and fitness level, with small group sizes. A full-day visit to Machu Picchu can be arranged as part of your stay; applicable entry permit and train transport fees may apply separately. Alcoholic beverages, individual spa treatments, and privately guided explorations are available at an additional cost.

faqs.q: How do I get to Explora Valle Sagrado from Cusco?
faqs.a: The lodge is approximately 90 kilometers from Alejandro Velasco Astete International Airport in Cusco (CUZ). Explora arranges round-trip airport transfers that should be confirmed at the time of booking. The drive from Cusco Airport to the lodge takes approximately 1.5 to 2 hours through the Andean highlands. Guests flying from abroad should book a connecting domestic flight to Cusco via Lima (LIM); the Lima-to-Cusco flight takes approximately 1 hour 20 minutes, with several daily connections available through major Peruvian carriers.

faqs.q: How far in advance should I book Explora Valle Sagrado?
faqs.a: Explora Valle Sagrado has 50 rooms, and demand from international travelers is consistent year-round. Booking four to six months in advance is recommended, particularly for the May through August dry season and the December through January peak period. Advance booking is also essential for the Machu Picchu component of any stay, as timed entry permits are required by the Peruvian government and can sell out several months ahead. Reservations can be made directly through Explora’s website or through a travel specialist.

faqs.q: Can you stay overnight at Machu Picchu?
faqs.a: There is no accommodation at the Machu Picchu archaeological site itself. The closest hotel is Belmond Sanctuary Lodge, located at the entrance gate to the ruins in Aguas Calientes — a town at the base of the mountain accessible by train from Cusco or Ollantaytambo. Most travelers visit Machu Picchu as a day trip from a base in the Sacred Valley or Cusco. Explora Valle Sagrado in the Sacred Valley offers a full-day guided excursion to Machu Picchu, included as part of the all-inclusive lodge rate, with train transport from Ollantaytambo and guided site access; entry permits are arranged in advance and may involve a separate fee.

faqs.q: Are guided excursions to Machu Picchu included in the Explora lodge rate?
faqs.a: A full-day visit to Machu Picchu is available as a guided exploration from Explora Valle Sagrado and can be arranged as part of any stay. The guided excursion — led by Explora’s bilingual guides — includes assistance with train logistics from Ollantaytambo and guided access at the site. The applicable Machu Picchu entry permit and train transport fees are charged separately, as these are set by the Peruvian government and the train operator. All other explorations across the Sacred Valley — including Pisac, Ollantaytambo, Chinchero, Moray, and the Maras salt mines — are fully included in the all-inclusive rate at no additional cost.

faqs.q: How is the climate in Cusco and when is the best time to travel?
faqs.a: The Sacred Valley enjoys two distinct seasons, each with its own character and appeal — shaped by the region’s high altitude and proximity to the equator. Dry Season (April – October) This is the sunniest time of year, with clear skies and crisp mountain air. The landscape takes on warm shades of yellow and ochre as the Andean plains dry out. Temperatures are pleasant during the day, ranging from 41°F to 68°F (5°C to 20°C), though nights can be cold and occasional frosts are not uncommon, sometimes dropping to 32°F (0°C). Wet Season (November – March) The valley transforms into a lush, vivid green as rainfall brings the landscape to life. The atmosphere is warmer and more subtropical, with temperatures ranging from 45°F to 70°F (7°C to 21°C). While rain is frequent, it rarely lasts all day — mornings are often clear, and the light during this season is particularly beautiful. Both seasons offer genuinely rewarding experiences, and the “best” time to visit ultimately depends on the kind of landscape and atmosphere you’re drawn to. We’re happy to help you decide based on your preferences.

faqs.q: How many nights do you recommend staying at Explora Sacred Valley?
faqs.a: We recommend a minimum of five nights to truly experience the Sacred Valley. The region is remarkably diverse, and a shorter stay simply doesn’t allow enough time to explore its many hidden corners and lesser-known sites. For those wishing to include our full-day explorations to Machu Picchu or Cusco — two of the highlights of any visit to this region — five nights is the baseline we suggest. If you’d like a deeper, more unhurried experience of both the Sacred Valley and the greater Cusco region, six nights is an excellent choice. Please note: Our Machu Picchu exploration combines Explora services with third-party providers, as required by the site’s access regulations. This excursion carries an additional cost depending on your program and must be confirmed with our reservations team at the time of booking.

faqs.q: What emergency medical services are available?
faqs.a: Guest safety is a priority at Explora. Most of our expert guides hold Wilderness First Responder (WFR) certification, equipping them with the skills and knowledge to respond effectively in remote environments. For medical emergencies requiring clinical attention, the nearby town of Urubamba — just a few kilometers from the lodge — has a Social Security Hospital as well as two local branches of established Cusco-based clinics: MAC Salud and CIMA Clinic. In the event of a severe case requiring more specialized care, patients are referred to facilities in Lima.

faqs.q: How can my relatives contact me in case of a emergency?
faqs.a: In case of an emergency, your relatives can reach the lodge directly by phone at +51 989 467 497 or by email at recvallesagrado@explora.com. Our front desk team is available around the clock to assist with any urgent communication.

faqs.q: Can I change the type of my bed on my room?
faqs.a: When making your reservation, you’ll be asked to choose between a king-size bed or a room with two double beds. If you’d like to change your bed configuration after booking, we’ll do our best to accommodate your request, subject to availability. We recommend reaching out to our reservations team as early as possible to ensure your preference is noted.

faqs.q: Do the rooms have air conditioning?
faqs.a: The Sacred Valley’s natural climate makes air conditioning unnecessary. Temperatures in the valley typically range between 9°C and 22°C (48°F and 72°F), creating a comfortable environment year-round. Beyond that, the lodge has been thoughtfully designed to make the most of natural ventilation and the area’s gentle air currents, keeping rooms fresh and pleasant throughout your stay.

faqs.q: What time do the transfers run between cusco airport and Explora?
faqs.a: Transfers between Cusco airport and Explora Sacred Valley are scheduled individually to align with each guest’s flight times, ensuring a seamless arrival and departure experience. For travelers not flying directly through Cusco airport, transfers operate according to a set timetable. Full details can be found on our Travel Tips page.

faqs.q: How can I arrange my exploration to Machu Picchu?
faqs.a: A visit to Machu Picchu is offered as a full-day overland exploration, featuring a guided tour of approximately three hours through the sanctuary’s most iconic archaeological sites. As access to the citadel is strictly limited, we strongly recommend coordinating this exploration with our reservations team well in advance — ideally at least four months ahead during high season. This allows us to secure your train tickets to Aguas Calientes, as well as your entrance to the citadel, both of which are subject to limited daily availability. Please note that specific schedules and routes within the site are also subject to availability at the time of booking. Please note: This exploration may carry an additional cost depending on your program.

faqs.q: Is there Wi-Fi?
faqs.a: As Explora Sacred Valley is nestled in a remote and pristine corner of the Andes, Wi-Fi connectivity is limited in both rooms and common areas. We invite you to embrace this as part of the experience — a rare opportunity to disconnect from the everyday and immerse yourself fully in the landscapes and culture of the Sacred Valley.

LAND OF ICE AND FIRE
ICELANDIC SAGAS
CULTURE AND FOLKLORE
Iceland’s geology is born from the interaction between fire and ice. Sitting atop the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart, the island is the stage for volcanic eruptions, rift valleys, and geothermal activity (the word “geyser” itself comes from Icelandic).
Eyjafjallajökull, the glacier-volcano famous for its 2010 eruption that paralyzed European air traffic, is connected to the magma chamber of nearby Katla and can trigger jökulhlaups (sudden glacial floods). To the south, Fjallabak stands out for the rhyolite mountains of Landmannalaugar and calderas such as Torfajökull.
With around 11 major glaciers, Iceland is home to Vatnajökull —Europe’s largest, covering 10% of the country— alongside Hofsjökull, Langjökull, and Mýrdalsjökull, the latter housing the subglacial volcano Grímsvötn. Its iconic waterfalls, shaped by glaciers, rivers, and volcanoes, complete a landscape as singular as it is essential to the country’s history.
Las sagas islandesas son narrativas épicas medievales (siglos XII–XIV) que combinan historia, mitología y leyenda, dando testimonio del espíritu de la Islandia medieval a través de temas como la colonización, la religión y las disputas familiares. Muchas transcurren en lugares específicos que aún hoy pueden visitarse, creando una conexión única entre historia y paisaje.
Más allá de su valor literario, las sagas documentan la vida social y legal de la época. Obras como la Saga de Njál y la Saga de Hrafnkell describen con maestría tanto las dinámicas humanas como los fenómenos naturales.
También registran eventos históricos como erupciones volcánicas: la Íslendinga Saga narra las erupciones de Reykjaneseldar (1210–1240) y sus estragos agrícolas, mientras que la Kristni Saga y la Saga de Njál las interpretan como señales de ira divina durante la conversión al cristianismo, mezclando geología y creencia religiosa.

Its iconic waterfalls, shaped by glaciers, rivers, and volcanoes, complete a landscape as singular as it is essential to the country’s history.

Muchas transcurren en lugares específicos que aún hoy pueden visitarse, creando una conexión única entre historia y paisaje. Icelandic folklore fuses mythology, nature, and tradition, reflecting its people’s deep connection to the land. Its stories are populated by beings that embody this bond with the supernatural. The Huldufólk (elves) dwell in rocks and hills, and belief in them still influences the country’s urban planning. Trolls—giants turned to stone by sunlight—personify nature’s dangers and mysteries. The Fjallkonan, “mountain woman,” symbolizes the very essence of the Icelandic landscape. Rooted in Norse and Celtic traditions, these tales—passed down through generations—have preserved the local language and customs, weaving together the physical and the spiritual. Stories like the Bergbúa þáttr imbue glaciers and mountains with supernatural meaning, testament to the unique relationship between Icelanders and their surroundings.

Day 5: Into the Highlands
Today, return to the Highlands to explore the aweinspiring Lakagígar region, the volcanic fissure responsible for the devastating European famine of 1783. This extraordinary day features the stunning Langisjor Lake, northern edge of the Vatnajokull ice cap, and the pristine beauty of the Fjallabak Nature Reserve. In addition, enjoy several scenic stops during the day’s three-and-a-half-hour drive.
Accommodation: Highlands Center Hotel
During the day the drive will take approximately 3.5 hours, with at least three scenic stops along the way. We will choose from five carefully crafted exploration options, tailored to the weather and the physical abilities of our travelers.

sections.heading: Day 6: Landmannalaugar
sections.text:
Day 6: Landmannalaugar
Begin the day by heading south to Landmannalaugar. Nestled within the Fjallabak Nature Reserve, this kaleidoscopic landscape is renowned for some of Iceland’s most iconic hiking trails. Today’s hikes are the most challenging of our journey, promising breathtaking discoveries and views. Inside the Fjallabak Nature Reserve, choose from four hiking options ranging from 1.5 miles (2.5 kilometers) to 12.4 miles (20 kilometers). Today’s three-hour drive reveals majestic scenery and stops along the way. Return to your hotel after an invigorating day.
Accommodation: Highlands Center Hotel
The drive will take approximately 3 hours, with three scenic stops along the way. Inside the Fjallabak Nature Reserve, we’ll choose from four hiking options ranging from 2.5 kilometers (1.5 miles) to 20 kilometers (12.4 miles).

Day 7: Valleys, Craters and Sky Lagoon

LAND OF ICE AND FIRE
ICELANDIC SAGAS
CULTURE AND FOLKLORE
Iceland’s geology is born from the interaction between fire and ice. Sitting atop the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart, the island is the stage for volcanic eruptions, rift valleys, and geothermal activity (the word “geyser” itself comes from Icelandic).
Eyjafjallajökull, the glacier-volcano famous for its 2010 eruption that paralyzed European air traffic, is connected to the magma chamber of nearby Katla and can trigger jökulhlaups (sudden glacial floods). To the south, Fjallabak stands out for the rhyolite mountains of Landmannalaugar and calderas such as Torfajökull.
With around 11 major glaciers, Iceland is home to Vatnajökull —Europe’s largest, covering 10% of the country— alongside Hofsjökull, Langjökull, and Mýrdalsjökull, the latter housing the subglacial volcano Grímsvötn. Its iconic waterfalls, shaped by glaciers, rivers, and volcanoes, complete a landscape as singular as it is essential to the country’s history.
Las sagas islandesas son narrativas épicas medievales (siglos XII–XIV) que combinan historia, mitología y leyenda, dando testimonio del espíritu de la Islandia medieval a través de temas como la colonización, la religión y las disputas familiares. Muchas transcurren en lugares específicos que aún hoy pueden visitarse, creando una conexión única entre historia y paisaje.
Más allá de su valor literario, las sagas documentan la vida social y legal de la época. Obras como la Saga de Njál y la Saga de Hrafnkell describen con maestría tanto las dinámicas humanas como los fenómenos naturales.
También registran eventos históricos como erupciones volcánicas: la Íslendinga Saga narra las erupciones de Reykjaneseldar (1210–1240) y sus estragos agrícolas, mientras que la Kristni Saga y la Saga de Njál las interpretan como señales de ira divina durante la conversión al cristianismo, mezclando geología y creencia religiosa.

sections.text:
THE MOUNTAINS
ANCIENT ROUTES
FLORA AND FAUNA
Sacred Mountains, The Apus
The Andean worldview interprets existence through deep observation of the natural environment. Ancient inhabitants tracked celestial patterns —the Earth’s orbit, the Moon’s movement, the stars— using this knowledge to understand seasonal cycles and shape both daily and spiritual life.
This worldview weaves together three dimensions: the scientific, the spiritual, and the mystical. Celestial observation allowed them to recognize equinoxes and solstices, managing time for agricultural, ceremonial, and social purposes.
At its heart lies a profound sense of the sacred, embodied by the Apus —sacred mountains revered as guardians and keepers of natural and spiritual balance. This bond is expressed through offerings and rituals, from simple gestures like coca leaves with sugar or chocolate, to elaborate ceremonies such as the pagos a la Madre Tierra (payments to Mother Earth), where agricultural products and symbolic items are offered as living reminders of humanity’s interdependence with nature.
The Apus also follow a hierarchy: in the Cusco region, Ausangate and Salkantay stand as the most prominent, joined by Verónica, Chicón, and Sawa Siray to form a network of sacred sites still honored today.
By uniting science, spirit, and mysticism, the Andean worldview reveals the wisdom of pre-Hispanic cultures and invites reflection on our own relationship with the natural world.
The Ancient routes and the Qhapaq Ñan
The Andean Road system spans nearly 30,000 kilometers from north to south and exceeds 60,000 kilometers when including its branches. This vast network integrates the ancestral pathways built by the Caral, Chavín, Huayri, and Quechua cultures, along with the Qhapaq Ñan, or “Path of the Lord,” which was laid over selected ancient routes and supplemented with infrastructure added to preexisting trails.

This bond is expressed through offerings and rituals, from simple gestures like coca leaves with sugar or chocolate, to elaborate ceremonies such as the pagos a la Madre Tierra (payments to Mother Earth), where agricultural products and symbolic items are offered as living reminders of humanity’s interdependence with nature. The Apus also follow a hierarchy: in the Cusco region, Ausangate and Salkantay stand as the most prominent, joined by Verónica, Chicón, and Sawa Siray to form a network of sacred sites still honored today. By uniting science, spirit, and mysticism, the Andean worldview reveals the wisdom of pre-Hispanic cultures and invites reflection on our own relationship with the natural world.

The Ancient routes and the Qhapaq Ñan The Andean Road system spans nearly 30,000 kilometers from north to south and exceeds 60,000 kilometers when including its branches. This vast network integrates the ancestral pathways built by the Caral, Chavín, Huayri, and Quechua cultures, along with the Qhapaq Ñan, or “Path of the Lord,” which was laid over selected ancient routes and supplemented with infrastructure added to preexisting trails. Starting from Cusco, road system extended towards the four cardinal directions, marking the territorial division of the Tahuantinsuyo. This system allowed access to the four suyos (Quechua suyu: ‘region’ or ‘territory’). The road system known as Qhapaq Ñan is “one of the most monumental achievements of human ingenuity, created in one of the planet’s most hostile natural environments. Due to its vast cultural, technical, and symbolic significance, this project conveys a powerful message to all nations of the world. It stands as a model of cultural cooperation.

During the Sacred Mountains expedition, travelers pass through diverse ecological zones, each offering unique flora and fauna. These range from cloud forests and the high Andean puna to the Sacred Valley, showcasing remarkable biodiversity and evolving landscapes. The cloud forest near Machu Picchu, rich in orchids, ferns, and mosses, is home to the elusive spectacled bear, alongside butterflies and birds. In the puna, at over 4,000 meters, resilient plants like ichu grass thrive, and rare sightings of pumas and condors add to its mystique. Transition zones, like the Suni plateau, feature native crops and recovering flora like the chaucha tree. Finally, the fertile Sacred Valley supports vibrant agriculture and occasional sightings of wildlife descending from higher elevations. This journey highlights the intricate relationship between nature and local communities, emphasizing the importance of conserving these unique ecosystems. Each zone reveals an inspiring story of biodiversity and adaptation across varied altitudes.

sections.heading: Expedition Itinerary
sections.text:
Expedition Itinerary
This expedition begins at Explora Valle Sagrado, where we gather at noon on the first day to meet and prepare for the adventure ahead. Over the following days, the itinerary takes you along ancient Inca paths, through breathtaking archaeological sites, and into awe-inspiring natural landscapes. You’ll connect with the Sacred Mountains of the Incas, culminating in an unforgettable arrival at the world-renowned sanctuary of Machu Picchu, entering through the iconic Intipunku Sun Gate.

sections.heading: Day 1 – The Adventure Begins
sections.text:
Day 1 – The Adventure Begins
Arrive at Cusco Airport, where you are transported to Explora Valle Sagrado. Gather to meet with fellow travelers, your guide, and the Expedition Leader for an introductory talk about the exciting journey ahead. Enjoy lunch at the lodge with your group, featuring a specially crafted menu to savor the local flavors of the Sacred Valley. Later, embark on your first Exploration with an overland journey to Chinchero and a 2.9-mile hike (4.6 km). Visit the archaeological site of Machu Kolka and hike through picturesque crop fields, offering stunning views of the pampas, Urquillos Valley, and surrounding snow-capped mountains.

Day 4 – Misquiyaco Private Conservation Area
This morning, we leave Explora Valle Sagrado and drive into the highlands of the Sacred Valley, watching the landscape open into wide plateaus and small farming communities before reaching the Misquiyaco Private Conservation Area—a protected buffer zone to Machu Picchu entered with exclusive Explora access. After meeting our camp team and muleteers, we begin a 4.8-mile hike (7.7 km) through the Sacred Mountains of the Incas, starting in a relict Mesoandean forest, gradually ascending beyond the tree line. We pause for a trail-side lunch, then continue on to our first tented campsite.

sections.heading: Day 5 – Sacred Salkantay Mountain
sections.text:
Day 5 – Sacred Salkantay Mountain
This morning, we set out on an 8.1-mile (13 km) mountain trek toward Apu Salkantay, the snow-capped giant of the Vilcabamba range. In Andean belief, Apus are revered as mountain guardians, and Salkantay is often regarded as one of the most significant among them. The route reaches a maximum altitude of 15,324 ft (4,671 m), opening wide views of ridgelines and valleys as we move deeper into the range. We end the day in Pampacahuana, settling into camp at 12,795 ft (3,900 m) for the night.

Day 6 – Descent Toward the Vilcanota River and the Sacred Valley
Today we descend through a long, scenic valley toward the Vilcanota River, gradually approaching the Sacred Valley once again. Along the way, we pass remnants of Inca agricultural terraces that reveal the ingenuity of ancient mountain farming. The route covers 15.2 km (9.4 mi) with a total descent of 1,308 m (4.291 ft), offering shifting landscapes as we lose altitude. We end the day at our new camp, Chamana, located at 2,575 m (8,448 ft), surrounded by a lush and tranquil Andean environment.

sections.text:
Day 7 – Journey to Ollantaytambo and Andean Traditions
This morning, we walk for around 2.5 hours through Andean scenery before meeting our vehicle and continuing to Ollantaytambo. We visit the Temple of the Sun and explore its monumental terraces and finely crafted Inca stonework, then walk into the village along narrow cobblestone streets to the main square. Here, we pause to take in daily life around small markets, community gatherings, and local crafts. Later, we transfer to our lodge just outside the village for a traditional pachamanca lunch, prepared earth-oven style with local ingredients. The afternoon is free to rest and enjoy the quieter side of the Sacred Valley.

sections.heading: Day 8 – Inca Trail to the Sun Gate and Machu Picchu
sections.text:
Day 8 – Inca Trail to the Sun Gate and Machu Picchu
After breakfast, we travel by van to the station and take the Vistadome train to the starting point of the Inca Trail. From Chachabamba, we begin a 6.5-mile (10.5 km) hike, ascending along lush mountain slopes into the cloud forest to reach Wiñay Wayna, a standout Inca site of steep terraces and finely crafted stonework. We then continue to Inti Punku, the Sun Gate and the historic entrance to Machu Picchu. We enter the sanctuary and explore its main areas with our guide, then descend to Machu Picchu Pueblo for the return train to Ollantaytambo and our transfer back to Explora Valle Sagrado for a farewell dinner.

faqs.q: What happens in case of an emergency?
faqs.a: In case of an emergency, our team is trained to handle a range of situations. Our guides are certified in first aid, allowing them to properly assess and manage any incident that requires medical attention. We have an emergency plan, satellite communication, oxygen assistance, and evacuation points along the entire route, so we are prepared for any contingency. Depending on where the evacuation takes place, basic medical care is available in Ollantaytambo or Urubamba. For more complex treatments, or depending on the severity of the case, a transfer to Cusco may be necessary for further medical attention. Please note that we do not supply medications. This duffel bag will be transported between camps by mules, allowing you to focus on enjoying the trek comfortably. Any additional luggage or items you do not wish to take to the camping nights can be securely stored at the Explora hotel.

faqs.a: During the expedition, we will use a combination of transportation methods to ensure comfort and efficiency. Transfers from the hotel to the starting points of the hikes will be done by vans, allowing us to reach the starting points comfortably. For more scenic routes, such as the journey from Ollantaytambo to Machu Picchu Village, round trip, we will take the train, which offers stunning views of the Andean landscape. Additionally, during the trekking stages, we will use horses and mules to transport the equipment and supplies between camps, allowing us to enjoy the trek without the burden of heavy backpacks.

The Andean worldview interprets existence through deep observation of the natural environment. Ancient inhabitants tracked celestial patterns —the Earth’s orbit, the Moon’s movement, the stars— using this knowledge to understand seasonal cycles and shape both daily and spiritual life.
This worldview weaves together three dimensions: the scientific, the spiritual, and the mystical. Celestial observation allowed them to recognize equinoxes and solstices, managing time for agricultural, ceremonial, and social purposes.
At its heart lies a profound sense of the sacred, embodied by the Apus —sacred mountains revered as guardians and keepers of natural and spiritual balance. This bond is expressed through offerings and rituals, from simple gestures like coca leaves with sugar or chocolate, to elaborate ceremonies such as the pagos a la Madre Tierra (payments to Mother Earth), where agricultural products and symbolic items are offered as living reminders of humanity’s interdependence with nature.
The Apus also follow a hierarchy: in the Cusco region, Ausangate and Salkantay stand as the most prominent, joined by Verónica, Chicón, and Sawa Siray to form a network of sacred sites still honored today.
By uniting science, spirit, and mysticism, the Andean worldview reveals the wisdom of pre-Hispanic cultures and invites reflection on our own relationship with the natural world.
The Ancient routes and the Qhapaq Ñan
The Andean Road system spans nearly 30,000 kilometers from north to south and exceeds 60,000 kilometers when including its branches. This vast network integrates the ancestral pathways built by the Caral, Chavín, Huayri, and Quechua cultures, along with the Qhapaq Ñan, or “Path of the Lord,” which was laid over selected ancient routes and supplemented with infrastructure added to preexisting trails.

## ITINERARY
Expedition Itinerary
This expedition begins at Explora Valle Sagrado, where we gather at noon on the first day to meet and prepare for the adventure ahead. Over the following days, the itinerary takes you along ancient Inca paths, through breathtaking archaeological sites, and into awe-inspiring natural landscapes. You’ll connect with the Sacred Mountains of the Incas, culminating in an unforgettable arrival at the world-renowned sanctuary of Machu Picchu, entering through the iconic Intipunku Sun Gate.
Day 1 – The Adventure Begins
Arrive at Cusco Airport, where you are transported to Explora Valle Sagrado. Gather to meet with fellow travelers, your guide, and the Expedition Leader for an introductory talk about the exciting journey ahead. Enjoy lunch at the lodge with your group, featuring a specially crafted menu to savor the local flavors of the Sacred Valley. Later, embark on your first Exploration with an overland journey to Chinchero and a 2.9-mile hike (4.6 km). Visit the archaeological site of Machu Kolka and hike through picturesque crop fields, offering stunning views of the pampas, Urquillos Valley, and surrounding snow-capped mountains.
Accommodation: Explora Valle Sagrado

4.6 km / 2.9 mi 3,933 masl / 12,979 fasl 236 m / 776 ft
Day 2 – Journey to Ancient Wata
Set out for a full day on the ancient Inca Qhapaq Ñan trail, exploring sections of the road network that once connected the Andes. The route leads to Wata, where pre-Incan and Incan remains sit high above the valley, offering a strong first sense of the region’s history and scale. Return to Explora Valle Sagrado in the late afternoon.
Accommodation: Explora Valle Sagrado

11.5 km / 7.1 mi 3,820 masl / 12,532 fasl 808 m / 2,650 ft
Day 3 – Shepherds’ Route between Lamay and Pisac
This day is designed for acclimatization before the expedition moves into mountain camps. The route follows old shepherd trails around lagoons that sustain nearby rural communities, with gentle slopes and shifting Andean scenery. Back at Explora Valle Sagrado, the afternoon focuses on practical preparation—reviewing equipment, packing strategy, and what to expect as the journey transitions to camp-supported trekking.
Accommodation: Explora Valle Sagrado
Distance Max. altitude Elevation gain
10.3 km / 6.6 mi 4,396 masl / 14,422 fasl 432 m / 1,417 ft
Day 4 – Misquiyaco Private Conservation Area
This morning, we leave Explora Valle Sagrado and drive into the highlands of the Sacred Valley, watching the landscape open into wide plateaus and small farming communities before reaching the Misquiyaco Private Conservation Area—a protected buffer zone to Machu Picchu entered with exclusive Explora access. After meeting our camp team and muleteers, we begin a 4.8-mile hike (7.7 km) through the Sacred Mountains of the Incas, starting in a relict Mesoandean forest, gradually ascending beyond the tree line. We pause for a trail-side lunch, then continue on to our first tented campsite.
Accommodation: Private Tented Camp.
Distance Max. altitude Elevation gain
7.7 km / 4.8 mi 4,297 masl / 14,097 fasl 1,207 masl / 3,959 ft
Day 5 – Sacred Salkantay Mountain
This morning, we set out on an 8.1-mile (13 km) mountain trek toward Apu Salkantay, the snow-capped giant of the Vilcabamba range. In Andean belief, Apus are revered as mountain guardians, and Salkantay is often regarded as one of the most significant among them. The route reaches a maximum altitude of 15,324 ft (4,671 m), opening wide views of ridgelines and valleys as we move deeper into the range. We end the day in Pampacahuana, settling into camp at 12,795 ft (3,900 m) for the night.
Accommodation: Private Tented Camp.

13 km / 8 mi 4,671 masl / 15,324 fasl 819 m / 2,687 ft
Day 6 – Descent Toward the Vilcanota River and the Sacred Valley
Today we descend through a long, scenic valley toward the Vilcanota River, gradually approaching the Sacred Valley once again. Along the way, we pass remnants of Inca agricultural terraces that reveal the ingenuity of ancient mountain farming. The route covers 15.2 km (9.4 mi) with a total descent of 1,308 m (4.291 ft), offering shifting landscapes as we lose altitude. We end the day at our new camp, Chamana, located at 2,575 m (8,448 ft), surrounded by a lush and tranquil Andean environment.
Accommodation: Private Tented Camp.

TIERRA DEL FUEGO HISTORY
WILD LIFE AT THE END OF THE WORLD
THE STRAIT OF MAGELLAN
Tierra del Fuego holds within its lands a fascinating history. At the southernmost tip of America, where fire and ice intertwine, lies this territory of untamed beauty and awe-inspiring landscapes. Since ancient times, the indigenous tribes of Yámanas and Selk’nam inhabited these inhospitable lands, bravely adapting to their hostile environment. Their rich cultures and ancestral traditions still resonate in its mists.
It was in 1520 when the Portuguese navigator, Fernando de Magallanes, spotted the lights of bonfires burning on the coast and named this region Tierra del Fuego. Since then, daring explorers and seekers of wealth ventured into these turbulent waters and wild lands in search of treasures and new trade routes. However, the region’s challenging nature and relentless weather conditions turned Tierra del Fuego into a feared and respected place.
In the 19th century, the gold rush, sheep wool production, and timber industry attracted numerous settlers. However, as time passed, the region transformed into a starting point for scientific expeditions and Antarctic explorations, becoming a gateway to the last edge of the world.
Today, Tierra del Fuego lures travelers with its wild and majestic nature. Its parks are home to unique places with lush forests, imposing mountains, ancient peat bogs, and pristine glaciers. Adventurers venture into these territories, feeling the wind of the end of the world with every step.
Tierra del Fuego, a land of contrasts, holds within the essence of its settlers a history full of courage and exploration. Through the centuries, it has witnessed the struggle of humankind to conquer and understand its surroundings.
In addition to the incredible King Penguins, a rich fauna exists throughout the island and fjords.

The Strait of Magellan is an important maritime route located at the southern tip of South America. In 1520, it was first navigated by a European vessel led by the Portuguese explorer Hernando de Magallanes. The Strait of Magellan connects the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, providing an alternative for trade and navigation between both oceans. The strait has an approximate length of 570 kilometers and a width that varies between 2 and 32 kilometers in different sections. Navigating through it poses challenges due to strong currents, intense winds, and ever-changing weather conditions in the region. Throughout the centuries, the Strait of Magellan has been used as a crucial route for maritime trade, especially during the era of sailing ships. It has also been the setting for numerous scientific expeditions and explorations. Today, the strait is traversed by cargo ships, cruise liners, and fishing vessels. Additionally, its natural beauty and historical significance attract people who wish to explore this fascinating maritime passage.

Expedition Itinerary
This journey has been designed so that you can discover this remote territory alongside our expert exploration team. This is a place where highways don’t exist, services are scarce, and there are still native settlers who arrived decades ago to colonize a pristine territory.

sections.heading: Day 1: Welcome
sections.text:
Day 1: Welcome
We will meet this day at the Yegua Loca Hotel in Punta Arenas, where we will be waiting for you.
Depending on your arrival time, you can explore the beautiful city of Punta Arenas while we prepare for the evening, where we will enjoy the introduction to our journey with our exploration team and a dinner to kick off the trip.
Accommodation: Yegua Loca Hotel

sections.heading: Day 2: Strait of Magellan and Pampa
sections.text:
Day 2: Strait of Magellan and Pampa
Rise at dawn for breakfast before departing by boat across the Strait of Magellan, the most important natural passage between the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans. Enjoy the fresh sea air as you witness this passage from the deck. When explorer Ferdinand Magellan discovered the island of Tierra del Fuego, he named it after the large bonfires he saw from the sea, likely lit by the indigenous Selk’nam people who inhabited the area. Arrive at the port of Porvenir, where we will take a brief tour of the city to learn about its history and culture. Your journey continues as you cross vast expanses of pampa and several estancias, with a stop to marvel at the island’s only king penguin colony. Enjoy lunch and connect with the culture of Tierra del Fuego. Later, arrive at our accommodation in a local estancia.
Accommodation: Local estancia (single rooms only)

widgets.activate: click the span (Bootstrap collapse; adds .show to its data-target); desktop copy usually already shows full text

sections.heading: Day 3: Transition to Patagonian Forest
sections.text:
Day 3: Transition to Patagonian Forest
Today you cross the border and the endless plains of pampa to enter the forests of Tierra del Fuego. Arrive at Karukinka Park, a private natural reserve spanning more than 741,000 acres (300,000 hectares) that seeks to preserve the native environment and raise awareness about the island’s biodiversity. Take a 4.3-mile (7 km) hike to Cerro Pietro Grande to admire its diverse ecosystems, as well as the effect of beavers on its forests. End the day at our cabin accommodations near Lake Fagnano. These special accommodations belong to the Genkowsky family, who welcome us upon arrival. Considered the last settlers on the island, they built roads, settled against all odds to live in this part of the planet, and share their stories with us firsthand.
Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (select cabins have outdoor bathrooms)

sections.heading: Day 4: Navigating the Patagonian Fjords
sections.text:
Day 4: Navigating the Patagonian Fjords
After an early breakfast, head to Caleta María, a bay that was previously only accessible by sea until 2014, when a new land route was developed. Today, we travel by boat to navigate to Parry Fjord and cross the Almirantazgo Sound, Tierra del Fuego’s first protected marine area. Enjoy a moderate hike along the fjord’s edge through forests overlooking the glaciers. In the afternoon, we return to the protected area of the Almirantazgo Sound, where we find sea elephants, leopard seals, and black-browed albatrosses. Disembark at Caleta María and return to Estancia Fagnano for dinner and a relaxing evening.
Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (select cabins have outdoor bathrooms)

sections.heading: Day 5: Mountains and Forests
sections.text:
Day 5: Mountains and Forests
Today, embark on an active, full-day adventure at Yendegaia National Park. This park is closed to visitors, but Explora has special access to explore a part of this wonderful park at the end of the world. Led by our expert guides, enjoy a full-day hike of advanced intensity through the park’s varied terrain and its high-altitude lagoons.
Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (select cabins have outdoor bathrooms)

sections.heading: Day 6: Andean Treeline
sections.text:
Day 6: Andean Treeline
Today’s Exploration takes you to the extreme southeast side of Karukinka Park for a moderate walk along the tree line. At the highest point of this walk, take in incredible views of the mountains, valleys, and an ecosystem that is home to the greatest variety of plants in all of Karukinka, as well as its greatest concentration of endemic plant species. Snow is always possible in the area, so exploring with snowshoes may be necessary. Return to the cabins this evening for a farewell dinner with your fellow travelers.
Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (select cabins have outdoor bathrooms)

FAQs
WHAT IS INCLUDED?
In this trip, everything is included: Accommodations and transfers detailed in the itinerary, meals, beverages, and guided explorations.
WHERE DO I NEED TO ARRIVE?
The journey starts in Punta Arenas and ends in Punta Arenas. To get to the city of Punta Arenas, you will need to take a flight from Santiago de Chile. The direct flight has an estimated duration of 4 hours.
WILL YOU PICK ME UP FROM THE AIRPORT?
If your arrival is on the same day as the start of the trip, we will pick you up from the airport starting at 10 am and take you to the hotel.
If you arrived the day before, we will pick you up from your accommodation in Punta Arenas where you are staying.
Please note that the check-in time is from 3:00 pm onwards
IS THERE PHONE SIGNAL AND WI-FI IN TIERRA DEL FUEGO?
The phone signal is intermittent and will only be available until the 3rd day of the trip.
On the last day, when returning to Pampa Guanaco, we will have signal again.
There is no freely available Wi-Fi. There will be satellite Wi-Fi available for emergency cases at the cabins in Estancia Lago Fagnano.
WILL WE CARRY SATELLITE PHONES?
Yes. For the safety of our travelers, we will have a satellite phone in one of the vehicles for exclusive use in case of emergencies.
WHAT ARE THE LODGING OPTIONS FOR THE JOURNEY?
There are different types of accommodation during the trip, as options in Tierra del Fuego are very limited. Therefore, we have selected those that best align with creating a deep experiential connection with the territory and can provide extraordinary value to our travelers.

WHAT TYPE OF TRANSPORTATION WILL WE USE?
We will use 4×4 trucks for both our travelers and our staff accompanying us on this journey.
The trucks are suitable for the road and various weather conditions that we may encounter.

faqs.q: What is included?
faqs.a: In this trip, everything is included: Accommodations and transfers detailed in the itinerary, meals, beverages, and guided explorations.

faqs.q: Where do I need to arrive?
faqs.a: The journey starts in Punta Arenas and ends in Punta Arenas. To get to the city of Punta Arenas, you will need to take a flight from Santiago de Chile. The direct flight has an estimated duration of 4 hours.

faqs.q: Will you pick me up from the airport?
faqs.a: If your arrival is on the same day as the start of the trip, we will pick you up from the airport starting at 10 am and take you to the hotel. If you arrived the day before, we will pick you up from your accommodation in Punta Arenas where you are staying. Please note that the check-in time is from 3:00 pm onwards

faqs.q: Is there phone signal and Wi-Fi in Tierra del Fuego?
faqs.a: The phone signal is intermittent and will only be available until the 3rd day of the trip. On the last day, when returning to Pampa Guanaco, we will have signal again. There is no freely available Wi-Fi. There will be satellite Wi-Fi available for emergency cases at the cabins in Estancia Lago Fagnano.

faqs.q: Will we carry satellite phones?
faqs.a: Yes. For the safety of our travelers, we will have a satellite phone in one of the vehicles for exclusive use in case of emergencies.

faqs.q: What are the lodging options for the Journey?
faqs.a: There are different types of accommodation during the trip, as options in Tierra del Fuego are very limited. Therefore, we have selected those that best align with creating a deep experiential connection with the territory and can provide extraordinary value to our travelers. First night: We will stay in Punta Arenas at a small hotel, a colonial house that keeps the local culture alive both in its decor and offerings.

faqs.q: What type of transportation will we use?
faqs.a: We will use 4×4 trucks for both our travelers and our staff accompanying us on this journey. The trucks are suitable for the road and various weather conditions that we may encounter.

faqs.q: How much luggage can I bring?
faqs.a: We recommend a maximum of 1 suitcase weighing up to 20 kg. The plane that will transport you back to Punta Arenas from Tierra del Fuego has limited capacity.

faqs.q: Is the return trip to Punta Arenas by plane included?
faqs.a: The transfer on a private plane from Tierra del Fuego to Punta Arenas is included and has an approximate flight duration of 1 hour. We do not include the return experience by land, which could take an additional 6 to 10 hours. In case of weather restrictions and the plane cannot take off, the return will be by land. We recommend you take this into consideration for your return flight from Punta Arenas to Santiago de Chile.

faqs.q: Can I modify the itinerary and explorations?
faqs.a: It is not possible to modify the itinerary or explorations, they may be adjusted or modified only due to season and weather conditions.

faqs.q: What type of person is this journey recommended for?
faqs.a: This trip is recommended for active individuals who are capable of hiking on uneven terrain, such as mud, rocks, snow, or peat bogs. Hikes of up to 10 kilometers with inclines and declines are included.

faqs.q: How will the food be?
faqs.a: The food during the trip consists of a unique menu with local components from Patagonia. There will be lamb roasts on a spit and other preparations that help us understand part of the local culture of Tierra del Fuego. Travelers with any type of food intolerance should inform us in advance to evaluate the adaptation of their meals. Excellent Chilean wines are included in the menu.

faqs.q: Will this journey be the same as going to an Explora?
faqs.a: It won’t be the same as going to an Explora. This trip takes place in a remote location with basic infrastructure, but we will accommodate it with different Explora touches for each and every moment.

faqs.q: What happens in case of an emergency?
faqs.a: In case of an emergency, our team is trained to handle a range of situations. Our guides are certified in first aid, allowing them to properly assess and manage any incident that requires medical attention. Basic medical care is available in the town of Porvenir. For other treatments, or depending on the severity of the case, a transfer to Punta Arenas may be necessary. Given the remote nature of this territory and the absence of nearby pharmacies, we strongly recommend that travelers bring an adequate supply of any personal medications for the entire duration of the expedition. Please note that we do not provide or administer medications. If you take prescription medication or have a specific medical condition, be sure to carry everything you may need.

faqs.q: Can I cancel my booking free of charge?
faqs.a: Yes. You may cancel up to 60 days before your check-in date free of fines.

faqs.q: What happens if I cancel less than 60 days before check-in?
faqs.a: The following conditions apply based on how close to check-in you cancel: 60 days or more before check-in: no fine 59–30 days before check-in: 50% fine 29–0 days before check-in: 100% fine

faqs.q: Do I need to sign anything before traveling?
faqs.a: Yes. The traveler must sign the flight disclaimer and exploration waiver.

faqs.q: Should I purchase travel insurance?
faqs.a: We recommend it. Travel insurance is advised in case an emergency evacuation is needed.

TIERRA DEL FUEGO HISTORY
WILD LIFE AT THE END OF THE WORLD
THE STRAIT OF MAGELLAN
Tierra del Fuego holds within its lands a fascinating history. At the southernmost tip of America, where fire and ice intertwine, lies this territory of untamed beauty and awe-inspiring landscapes. Since ancient times, the indigenous tribes of Yámanas and Selk’nam inhabited these inhospitable lands, bravely adapting to their hostile environment. Their rich cultures and ancestral traditions still resonate in its mists.
It was in 1520 when the Portuguese navigator, Fernando de Magallanes, spotted the lights of bonfires burning on the coast and named this region Tierra del Fuego. Since then, daring explorers and seekers of wealth ventured into these turbulent waters and wild lands in search of treasures and new trade routes. However, the region’s challenging nature and relentless weather conditions turned Tierra del Fuego into a feared and respected place.
In the 19th century, the gold rush, sheep wool production, and timber industry attracted numerous settlers. However, as time passed, the region transformed into a starting point for scientific expeditions and Antarctic explorations, becoming a gateway to the last edge of the world.
Today, Tierra del Fuego lures travelers with its wild and majestic nature. Its parks are home to unique places with lush forests, imposing mountains, ancient peat bogs, and pristine glaciers. Adventurers venture into these territories, feeling the wind of the end of the world with every step.
Tierra del Fuego, a land of contrasts, holds within the essence of its settlers a history full of courage and exploration. Through the centuries, it has witnessed the struggle of humankind to conquer and understand its surroundings.
In addition to the incredible King Penguins, a rich fauna exists throughout the island and fjords.

## ITINERARY
Expedition Itinerary
This journey has been designed so that you can discover this remote territory alongside our expert exploration team. This is a place where highways don’t exist, services are scarce, and there are still native settlers who arrived decades ago to colonize a pristine territory.
Day 1: Welcome
We will meet this day at the Yegua Loca Hotel in Punta Arenas, where we will be waiting for you.
Depending on your arrival time, you can explore the beautiful city of Punta Arenas while we prepare for the evening, where we will enjoy the introduction to our journey with our exploration team and a dinner to kick off the trip.
Accommodation: Yegua Loca Hotel
Day 2: Strait of Magellan and Pampa
Rise at dawn for breakfast before departing by boat across the Strait of Magellan, the most important natural passage between the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans. Enjoy the fresh sea air as you witness this passage from the deck. When explorer Ferdinand Magellan discovered the island of Tierra del Fuego, he named it after the large bonfires he saw from the sea, likely lit by the indigenous Selk’nam people who inhabited the area. Arrive at the port of Porvenir, where we will take a brief tour of the city to learn about its history and culture. Your journey continues as you cross vast expanses of pampa and several estancias, with a stop to marvel at the island’s only king penguin colony. Enjoy lunch and connect with the culture of Tierra del Fuego. Later, arrive at our accommodation in a local estancia.
Accommodation: Local estancia (single rooms only)
Day 3: Transition to Patagonian Forest
Today you cross the border and the endless plains of pampa to enter the forests of Tierra del Fuego. Arrive at Karukinka Park, a private natural reserve spanning more than 741,000 acres (300,000 hectares) that seeks to preserve the native environment and raise awareness about the island’s biodiversity. Take a 4.3-mile (7 km) hike to Cerro Pietro Grande to admire its diverse ecosystems, as well as the effect of beavers on its forests. End the day at our cabin accommodations near Lake Fagnano. These special accommodations belong to the Genkowsky family, who welcome us upon arrival. Considered the last settlers on the island, they built roads, settled against all odds to live in this part of the planet, and share their stories with us firsthand.
Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (select cabins have outdoor bathrooms)
Day 4: Navigating the Patagonian Fjords
After an early breakfast, head to Caleta María, a bay that was previously only accessible by sea until 2014, when a new land route was developed. Today, we travel by boat to navigate to Parry Fjord and cross the Almirantazgo Sound, Tierra del Fuego’s first protected marine area. Enjoy a moderate hike along the fjord’s edge through forests overlooking the glaciers. In the afternoon, we return to the protected area of the Almirantazgo Sound, where we find sea elephants, leopard seals, and black-browed albatrosses. Disembark at Caleta María and return to Estancia Fagnano for dinner and a relaxing evening.
Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (select cabins have outdoor bathrooms)
Day 5: Mountains and Forests
Today, embark on an active, full-day adventure at Yendegaia National Park. This park is closed to visitors, but Explora has special access to explore a part of this wonderful park at the end of the world. Led by our expert guides, enjoy a full-day hike of advanced intensity through the park’s varied terrain and its high-altitude lagoons.
Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (select cabins have outdoor bathrooms)
Day 6: Andean Treeline
Today’s Exploration takes you to the extreme southeast side of Karukinka Park for a moderate walk along the tree line. At the highest point of this walk, take in incredible views of the mountains, valleys, and an ecosystem that is home to the greatest variety of plants in all of Karukinka, as well as its greatest concentration of endemic plant species. Snow is always possible in the area, so exploring with snowshoes may be necessary. Return to the cabins this evening for a farewell dinner with your fellow travelers.
Accommodation: Estancia Fagnano (select cabins have outdoor bathrooms)

LAND OF ICE AND FIRE
ICELANDIC SAGAS
CULTURE AND FOLKLORE
Iceland’s geology is born from the interaction between fire and ice. Sitting atop the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart, the island is the stage for volcanic eruptions, rift valleys, and geothermal activity (the word “geyser” itself comes from Icelandic).
Eyjafjallajökull, the glacier-volcano famous for its 2010 eruption that paralyzed European air traffic, is connected to the magma chamber of nearby Katla and can trigger jökulhlaups (sudden glacial floods). To the south, Fjallabak stands out for the rhyolite mountains of Landmannalaugar and calderas such as Torfajökull.
With around 11 major glaciers, Iceland is home to Vatnajökull —Europe’s largest, covering 10% of the country— alongside Hofsjökull, Langjökull, and Mýrdalsjökull, the latter housing the subglacial volcano Grímsvötn. Its iconic waterfalls, shaped by glaciers, rivers, and volcanoes, complete a landscape as singular as it is essential to the country’s history.
Las sagas islandesas son narrativas épicas medievales (siglos XII–XIV) que combinan historia, mitología y leyenda, dando testimonio del espíritu de la Islandia medieval a través de temas como la colonización, la religión y las disputas familiares. Muchas transcurren en lugares específicos que aún hoy pueden visitarse, creando una conexión única entre historia y paisaje.
Más allá de su valor literario, las sagas documentan la vida social y legal de la época. Obras como la Saga de Njál y la Saga de Hrafnkell describen con maestría tanto las dinámicas humanas como los fenómenos naturales.
También registran eventos históricos como erupciones volcánicas: la Íslendinga Saga narra las erupciones de Reykjaneseldar (1210–1240) y sus estragos agrícolas, mientras que la Kristni Saga y la Saga de Njál las interpretan como señales de ira divina durante la conversión al cristianismo, mezclando geología y creencia religiosa.

Icelandic folklore fuses mythology, nature, and tradition, reflecting its people’s deep connection to the land. Its stories are populated by beings that embody this bond with the supernatural. The Huldufólk (elves) dwell in rocks and hills, and belief in them still influences the country’s urban planning. Trolls—giants turned to stone by sunlight—personify nature’s dangers and mysteries. The Fjallkonan, “mountain woman,” symbolizes the very essence of the Icelandic landscape. Rooted in Norse and Celtic traditions, these tales—passed down through generations—have preserved the local language and customs, weaving together the physical and the spiritual. Stories like the Bergbúa þáttr imbue glaciers and mountains with supernatural meaning, testament to the unique relationship between Icelanders and their surroundings.

Ride snowmobiles toward the volcanic summit of Eyjafjallajökull — silent now, but far from dormant. THE MOUNTAINS
ANCIENT ROUTES
FLORA AND FAUNA
Sacred Mountains, The Apus
The Andean worldview interprets existence through deep observation of the natural environment. Ancient inhabitants tracked celestial patterns —the Earth’s orbit, the Moon’s movement, the stars— using this knowledge to understand seasonal cycles and shape both daily and spiritual life.
This worldview weaves together three dimensions: the scientific, the spiritual, and the mystical. Celestial observation allowed them to recognize equinoxes and solstices, managing time for agricultural, ceremonial, and social purposes.
At its heart lies a profound sense of the sacred, embodied by the Apus —sacred mountains revered as guardians and keepers of natural and spiritual balance. This bond is expressed through offerings and rituals, from simple gestures like coca leaves with sugar or chocolate, to elaborate ceremonies such as the pagos a la Madre Tierra (payments to Mother Earth), where agricultural products and symbolic items are offered as living reminders of humanity’s interdependence with nature.
The Apus also follow a hierarchy: in the Cusco region, Ausangate and Salkantay stand as the most prominent, joined by Verónica, Chicón, and Sawa Siray to form a network of sacred sites still honored today.
By uniting science, spirit, and mysticism, the Andean worldview reveals the wisdom of pre-Hispanic cultures and invites reflection on our own relationship with the natural world.
The Ancient routes and the Qhapaq Ñan
The Andean Road system spans nearly 30,000 kilometers from north to south and exceeds 60,000 kilometers when including its branches. This vast network integrates the ancestral pathways built by the Caral, Chavín, Huayri, and Quechua cultures, along with the Qhapaq Ñan, or “Path of the Lord,” which was laid over selected ancient routes and supplemented with infrastructure added to preexisting trails.

The Ancient routes and the Qhapaq Ñan The Andean Road system spans nearly 30,000 kilometers from north to south and exceeds 60,000 kilometers when including its branches. This vast network integrates the ancestral pathways built by the Caral, Chavín, Huayri, and Quechua cultures, along with the Qhapaq Ñan, or “Path of the Lord,” which was laid over selected ancient routes and supplemented with infrastructure added to preexisting trails. Starting from Cusco, road system extended towards the four cardinal directions, marking the territorial division of the Tahuantinsuyo. This system allowed access to the four suyos (Quechua suyu: ‘region’ or ‘territory’). The road system known as Qhapaq Ñan is “one of the most monumental achievements of human ingenuity, created in one of the planet’s most hostile natural environments. Due to its vast cultural, technical, and symbolic significance, this project conveys a powerful message to all nations of the world. It stands as a model of cultural cooperation.

During the Sacred Mountains expedition, travelers pass through diverse ecological zones, each offering unique flora and fauna. These range from cloud forests and the high Andean puna to the Sacred Valley, showcasing remarkable biodiversity and evolving landscapes. The cloud forest near Machu Picchu, rich in orchids, ferns, and mosses, is home to the elusive spectacled bear, alongside butterflies and birds. In the puna, at over 4,000 meters, resilient plants like ichu grass thrive, and rare sightings of pumas and condors add to its mystique. Transition zones, like the Suni plateau, feature native crops and recovering flora like the chaucha tree. Finally, the fertile Sacred Valley supports vibrant agriculture and occasional sightings of wildlife descending from higher elevations. This journey highlights the intricate relationship between nature and local communities, emphasizing the importance of conserving these unique ecosystems. Each zone reveals an inspiring story of biodiversity and adaptation across varied altitudes.

TIERRA DEL FUEGO HISTORY
WILD LIFE AT THE END OF THE WORLD
THE STRAIT OF MAGELLAN
Tierra del Fuego holds within its lands a fascinating history. At the southernmost tip of America, where fire and ice intertwine, lies this territory of untamed beauty and awe-inspiring landscapes. Since ancient times, the indigenous tribes of Yámanas and Selk’nam inhabited these inhospitable lands, bravely adapting to their hostile environment. Their rich cultures and ancestral traditions still resonate in its mists.
It was in 1520 when the Portuguese navigator, Fernando de Magallanes, spotted the lights of bonfires burning on the coast and named this region Tierra del Fuego. Since then, daring explorers and seekers of wealth ventured into these turbulent waters and wild lands in search of treasures and new trade routes. However, the region’s challenging nature and relentless weather conditions turned Tierra del Fuego into a feared and respected place.
In the 19th century, the gold rush, sheep wool production, and timber industry attracted numerous settlers. However, as time passed, the region transformed into a starting point for scientific expeditions and Antarctic explorations, becoming a gateway to the last edge of the world.
Today, Tierra del Fuego lures travelers with its wild and majestic nature. Its parks are home to unique places with lush forests, imposing mountains, ancient peat bogs, and pristine glaciers. Adventurers venture into these territories, feeling the wind of the end of the world with every step.
Tierra del Fuego, a land of contrasts, holds within the essence of its settlers a history full of courage and exploration. Through the centuries, it has witnessed the struggle of humankind to conquer and understand its surroundings.
In addition to the incredible King Penguins, a rich fauna exists throughout the island and fjords.

The Strait of Magellan is an important maritime route located at the southern tip of South America. In 1520, it was first navigated by a European vessel led by the Portuguese explorer Hernando de Magallanes. The Strait of Magellan connects the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, providing an alternative for trade and navigation between both oceans. The strait has an approximate length of 570 kilometers and a width that varies between 2 and 32 kilometers in different sections. Navigating through it poses challenges due to strong currents, intense winds, and ever-changing weather conditions in the region. Throughout the centuries, the Strait of Magellan has been used as a crucial route for maritime trade, especially during the era of sailing ships. It has also been the setting for numerous scientific expeditions and explorations. Today, the strait is traversed by cargo ships, cruise liners, and fishing vessels. Additionally, its natural beauty and historical significance attract people who wish to explore this fascinating maritime passage.

LAND OF ICE AND FIRE
ICELANDIC SAGAS
CULTURE AND FOLKLORE
Iceland’s geology is born from the interaction between fire and ice. Sitting atop the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart, the island is the stage for volcanic eruptions, rift valleys, and geothermal activity (the word “geyser” itself comes from Icelandic).
Eyjafjallajökull, the glacier-volcano famous for its 2010 eruption that paralyzed European air traffic, is connected to the magma chamber of nearby Katla and can trigger jökulhlaups (sudden glacial floods). To the south, Fjallabak stands out for the rhyolite mountains of Landmannalaugar and calderas such as Torfajökull.
With around 11 major glaciers, Iceland is home to Vatnajökull —Europe’s largest, covering 10% of the country— alongside Hofsjökull, Langjökull, and Mýrdalsjökull, the latter housing the subglacial volcano Grímsvötn. Its iconic waterfalls, shaped by glaciers, rivers, and volcanoes, complete a landscape as singular as it is essential to the country’s history.
Las sagas islandesas son narrativas épicas medievales (siglos XII–XIV) que combinan historia, mitología y leyenda, dando testimonio del espíritu de la Islandia medieval a través de temas como la colonización, la religión y las disputas familiares. Muchas transcurren en lugares específicos que aún hoy pueden visitarse, creando una conexión única entre historia y paisaje.
Más allá de su valor literario, las sagas documentan la vida social y legal de la época. Obras como la Saga de Njál y la Saga de Hrafnkell describen con maestría tanto las dinámicas humanas como los fenómenos naturales.
También registran eventos históricos como erupciones volcánicas: la Íslendinga Saga narra las erupciones de Reykjaneseldar (1210–1240) y sus estragos agrícolas, mientras que la Kristni Saga y la Saga de Njál las interpretan como señales de ira divina durante la conversión al cristianismo, mezclando geología y creencia religiosa.

Day 1: Reykjavik
The first night in Iceland is always one of orientation. Hotel Borg in the historic heart — 1930s Art Déco architecture that signals this is no ordinary trip. The group aperitif is the opening ritual: sharing expectations, aligning on the expedition mindset. What strikes most in Reykjavik in winter is the darkness — barely 5 hours of daylight — and the possibility of seeing the Northern Lights from the city itself.

The temperatures in Iceland’s broad variety of landscapes vary considerably. That is why it’s very important to be prepared when exploring its vast territories. Explora provides trekking poles and a reusable water bottle, and will provide additional personal safety equipment when required during explorations.

Outer layer: Waterproof and windproof jacket and pants
